steps.text: Find the acceleration of the blocks, in m/s².

items.description: mass of the uniform disc pulley
items.name: M

items: g is a uniform constant of the stated value.
The string is light and inextensible and does not slip on the pulley.
The pulley is a uniform solid disc turning without axle friction.

steps.text: Apply Newton's second law to each hanging block and the rotational form of the second law to the pulley, with the string not slipping. Combining them gives one equation of motion for the whole system, in which the pulley adds an effective mass.

steps.description: effective inertial mass of the system
steps.principle: Newton's second law for each block, the rotational law tau = I alpha with I = (1/2) M R^2 for the disc, and the no-slip condition a = alpha R
steps.why: The two tensions differ because the pulley has inertia: (T2 - T1) R = (1/2) M R^2 (a / R), so T2 - T1 = (M/2) a. Adding the block equations then shows that the whole system accelerates as if it had the inertial mass m1 + m2 + M/2.

steps.description: acceleration of the blocks
steps.principle: Newton's second law for the system: net driving force = effective mass x acceleration
steps.why: The net force along the string is the difference of the weights, (m2 - m1) g, and it must accelerate the effective inertial mass; dividing gives the common acceleration of the blocks.

steps.text: Taking M to zero gives the ideal Atwood result (m2 - m1) g / (m1 + m2), and equal masses give zero acceleration. The acceleration is always smaller than g, and the units N / kg give m/s^2.
acceleration of the blocks: 2.178 m/s²

Step 2. Given: m1 = 3 kg (mass of the left block; given); m2 = 5 kg (mass of the right block; given); M = 2 kg (mass of the uniform disc pulley; given); g = 9.8 m/s² (gravitational acceleration, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: g is a uniform constant of the stated value. The string is light and inextensible and does not slip on the pulley. The pulley is a uniform solid disc turning without axle friction.
Step 4. Approach: Apply Newton's second law to each hanging block and the rotational form of the second law to the pulley, with the string not slipping. Combining them gives one equation of motion for the whole system, in which the pulley adds an effective mass.
Step 5. Newton's second law for each block, the rotational law tau = I alpha with I = (1/2) M R^2 for the disc, and the no-slip condition a = alpha R. Step 8. Answer: acceleration of the blocks: 2.178 m/s².

steps.text: Find the voltage across the capacitor, in V.

items: The capacitor is initially uncharged.
The battery and wires are ideal and the capacitor does not leak.

steps.text: The capacitor charges exponentially toward the battery emf with a time constant set by the resistance and the capacitance. Find the time constant, express the elapsed time in units of it, and then evaluate the charging law.

steps.description: time constant
steps.principle: The RC time constant: tau = R C, the product of the series resistance and the capacitance
steps.why: The loop equation for the charging circuit contains only the combination R C as a time scale, so it sets how fast the capacitor voltage approaches the emf.

steps.description: elapsed time in units of the time constant
steps.principle: Dimensionless time: the elapsed time divided by the time constant, x = t/tau
steps.why: The charging law depends on time only through this ratio, so computing it first makes the final evaluation a one-line exponential.

steps.description: capacitor voltage
steps.principle: The charging law of an RC circuit, from Kirchhoff's loop rule V0 = I R + q/C with q = 0 at the start: V_C = V0 (1 - e^(-t/tau))
steps.why: The capacitor starts uncharged and is charged through the resistor from an ideal battery, so its voltage rises from zero toward V0 and at time t equals V0 times one minus the decaying exponential.

steps.text: At t = 0 the formula gives zero, at very long times it approaches the emf, and at t = tau it gives about 63 percent of the emf, so the answer must lie between zero and V0 and be larger the larger x is.
voltage across the capacitor: 6.608 V

steps.text: The capacitor charges exponentially toward the battery emf with a time constant set by the resistance and the capacitance. Find the time constant, express the elapsed time in units of it, and then evaluate the charging law.

steps.description: time constant
steps.principle: The RC time constant: tau = R C, the product of the series resistance and the capacitance
steps.why: The loop equation for the charging circuit contains only the combination R C as a time scale, so it sets how fast the capacitor voltage approaches the emf.

steps.description: elapsed time in units of the time constant
steps.principle: Dimensionless time: the elapsed time divided by the time constant, x = t/tau
steps.why: The charging law depends on time only through this ratio, so computing it first makes the final evaluation a one-line exponential.

steps.description: capacitor voltage
steps.principle: The charging law of an RC circuit, from Kirchhoff's loop rule V0 = I R + q/C with q = 0 at the start: V_C = V0 (1 - e^(-t/tau))
steps.why: The capacitor starts uncharged and is charged through the resistor from an ideal battery, so its voltage rises from zero toward V0 and at time t equals V0 times one minus the decaying exponential.

steps.text: At t = 0 the formula gives zero, at very long times it approaches the emf, and at t = tau it gives about 63 percent of the emf, so the answer must lie between zero and V0 and be larger the larger x is.
voltage across the capacitor: 6.608 V

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the voltage across the capacitor, in V.
Step 2. Given: V0 = 12 V (battery emf; given); R = 5 kΩ (series resistance; given); C = 20 μF (capacitance; given); t = 80 ms (time after the connection; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The capacitor is initially uncharged. The battery and wires are ideal and the capacitor does not leak.
Step 4. Approach: The capacitor charges exponentially toward the battery emf with a time constant set by the resistance and the capacitance. Find the time constant, express the elapsed time in units of it, and then evaluate the charging law.
Step 5. The RC time constant: tau = R C, the product of the series resistance and the capacitance. The loop equation for the charging circuit contains only the combination R C as a time scale, so it sets how fast the capacitor voltage approaches the emf. tau = R*C  (SI units). tau = (5000)*(2e-05) = 0.1 (SI) = 0.1 s.
Step 6. Dimensionless time: the elapsed time divided by the time constant, x = t/tau. The charging law depends on time only through this ratio, so computing it first makes the final evaluation a one-line exponential. x = t/tau  (SI units). x = (0.08)/(0.1) = 0.8 (SI) = 0.8.
Step 7. The charging law of an RC circuit, from Kirchhoff's loop rule V0 = I R + q/C with q = 0 at the start: V_C = V0 (1 - e^(-t/tau)). The capacitor starts uncharged and is charged through the resistor from an ideal battery, so its voltage rises from zero toward V0 and at time t equals V0 times one minus the decaying exponential. VC = V0*(1 - exp(-x))  (SI units). VC = (12)*(1 - exp(-(0.8))) = 6.608 (SI) = 6.608 V.
Step 8. Check: At t = 0 the formula gives zero, at very long times it approaches the emf, and at t = tau it gives about 63 percent of the emf, so the answer must lie between zero and V0 and be larger the larger x is.
Step 9. Answer: voltage across the capacitor: 6.608 V.

steps.text: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.

steps.description: mean translational kinetic energy of one mole of molecules
steps.principle: Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T
steps.why: The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone.

steps.description: root-mean-square speed of the molecules
steps.principle: Definition of the root-mean-square speed through the mean kinetic energy, (1/2) M v_rms^2 = Ek per mole
steps.why: The mean kinetic energy per mole equals half the molar mass times the mean square speed, and the rms speed is the square root of that mean square, so v_rms = sqrt(2 Ek / M); the molar mass must be in kilograms per mole.

steps.text: The result equals sqrt(3 R T / M), the standard kinetic-theory formula. Lighter molecules are faster at the same temperature, the speed grows as the square root of the absolute temperature, and typical speeds are of the order of hundreds of metres per second, comparable to the speed of sound.
root-mean-square speed of the molecules: 1368 m/s

items: The constant hc has the stated value and is used for every photon energy and wavelength.
The electron rest energy has the stated value.
The electron starts from rest and its kinetic energy is small compared with its rest energy, so the non-relativistic relation applies.
The de Broglie relation wavelength = h / momentum gives the wavelength of the electron.

steps.text: The question asks for the de Broglie wavelength of an electron whose kinetic energy is known. Find the momentum (multiplied by c so that it is an energy) from the kinetic energy, then apply lambda = h / p in the form hc / (p c).

steps.description: momentum of the electron multiplied by the speed of light
steps.principle: Non-relativistic kinetic energy K = p^2 / (2 m), so p c = sqrt(2 (m c^2) K).
steps.why: The electron started from rest, so the whole energy it gained is kinetic, and K is far below the rest energy, so the classical formula holds; solving for p and multiplying by c gives a momentum in energy units that matches hc.

steps.description: de Broglie wavelength of the electron
steps.principle: de Broglie relation: a particle of momentum p has the wavelength lambda = h / p = h c / (p c).
steps.why: Matter behaves as a wave with a wavelength set by its momentum, so dividing the stated hc by p c gives the wavelength directly in length units.

steps.text: The wavelength falls as one over the square root of the kinetic energy, so more energy gives a shorter wavelength. Dimensionally, hc is energy times length and p c is an energy, so the ratio is a length. For tens to hundreds of electronvolts the result is of the order of atomic spacings, which is why electrons of this energy diffract from crystals.
de Broglie wavelength of the electron: 100.1 pm

Step 3. Assumptions: The constant hc has the stated value and is used for every photon energy and wavelength. The electron rest energy has the stated value. items: The constant hc has the stated value and is used for every photon energy and wavelength.
The electron rest energy has the stated value.
The electron starts from rest and its kinetic energy is small compared with its rest energy, so the non-relativistic relation applies.

steps.text: The added sentence ("Before the wavelength is determined, an extra amount of kinetic energy is given to the proton by one more accelerating stage.") contains no number: there is no quantity to use, so the problem is the base problem.

The question asks for the de Broglie wavelength of an electron whose kinetic energy is known. Find the momentum (multiplied by c so that it is an energy) from the kinetic energy, then apply lambda = h / p in the form hc / (p c).

steps.description: momentum of the electron multiplied by the speed of light
steps.principle: Non-relativistic kinetic energy K = p^2 / (2 m), so p c = sqrt(2 (m c^2) K).
steps.why: The electron started from rest, so the whole energy it gained is kinetic, and K is far below the rest energy, so the classical formula holds; solving for p and multiplying by c gives a momentum in energy units that matches hc.

steps.description: de Broglie wavelength of the electron
steps.principle: de Broglie relation: a particle of momentum p has the wavelength lambda = h / p = h c / (p c).
steps.why: Matter behaves as a wave with a wavelength set by its momentum, so dividing the stated hc by p c gives the wavelength directly in length units.

steps.text: The wavelength falls as one over the square root of the kinetic energy, so more energy gives a shorter wavelength. Dimensionally, hc is energy times length and p c is an energy, so the ratio is a length. For tens to hundreds of electronvolts the result is of the order of atomic spacings, which is why electrons of this energy diffract from crystals.
de Broglie wavelength of the electron: 100.1 pm

Step 2. Given: Ke = 150 eV (kinetic energy gained by the electron; given); hc = 1240 eV*nm (Planck constant times the speed of light, a stated constant; stated constant); mc2 = 511 keV (rest energy of the electron, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The constant hc has the stated value and is used for every photon energy and wavelength. The electron rest energy has the stated value. The electron starts from rest and its kinetic energy is small compared with its rest energy, so the non-relativistic relation applies. The de Broglie relation wavelength = h / momentum gives the wavelength of the electron.
Step 4. The added sentence ("Before the wavelength is determined, an extra amount of kinetic energy is given to the proton by one more accelerating stage.") contains no number: there is no quantity to use, so the problem is the base problem.
Step 5. Approach: The question asks for the de Broglie wavelength of an electron whose kinetic energy is known. Find the momentum (multiplied by c so that it is an energy) from the kinetic energy, then apply lambda = h / p in the form hc / (p c).
Step 6. Non-relativistic kinetic energy K = p^2 / (2 m), so p c = sqrt(2 (m c^2) K). The electron started from rest, so the whole energy it gained is kinetic, and K is far below the rest energy, so the classical formula holds; solving for p and multiplying by c gives a momentum in energy units that matches hc. pc = sqrt(2*mc2*Ke)  (SI units). pc = sqrt(2*(8.187e-14)*(2.403e-17)) = 1.984e-15 (SI) = 1.238e+04 eV.
Step 7. de Broglie relation: a particle of momentum p has the wavelength lambda = h / p = h c / (p c). Matter behaves as a wave with a wavelength set by its momentum, so dividing the stated hc by p c gives the wavelength directly in length units. lamdb = hc/pc  (SI units). lamdb = (1.987e-25)/(1.984e-15) = 1.001e-10 (SI) = 100.1 pm.
Step 8. Check: The wavelength falls as one over the square root of the kinetic energy, so more energy gives a shorter wavelength. Dimensionally, hc is energy times length and p c is an energy, so the ratio is a length. For tens to hundreds of electronvolts the result is of the order of atomic spacings, which is why electrons of this energy diffract from crystals.
Step 9. Answer: de Broglie wavelength of the electron: 100.1 pm.

steps.why: The cube is completely under the surface, so it displaces exactly its own volume of liquid. Both its weight and the buoyant force are proportional to this volume, so we need it first.

steps.description: buoyant force on the cube
steps.principle: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid, Fb = rho_l g V
steps.why: The cube is fully submerged, so the displaced liquid has the volume of the cube and the density of the liquid. This is the upward force the liquid exerts on the cube; it needs the volume but not the mass.

steps.description: mass of the cube
steps.principle: Definition of density, rho = m / V, so m = rho_s V
steps.why: The weight of the cube is its mass times g, and the problem gives its density instead of its mass; the density times the volume gives the mass.

steps.description: tension in the string
steps.principle: Newton's first law for a body in equilibrium: the net vertical force is zero, Fb = m g + T
steps.why: The cube is at rest, and the string is tied to the bottom of the tank, so it pulls the cube down along with its weight. The upward buoyant force must balance both, so the tension is the buoyant force minus the weight.

steps.text: Limiting case: if the density of the cube equalled that of the liquid, the buoyant force would equal the weight and the tension would be zero; the tension is positive only when the cube is less dense than the liquid, as it must be for a cube that needs to be held down. The result scales with the cube volume and with the density difference.
tension in the string: 3.92 N

The cube is at rest, so the forces on it balance: the buoyant force of the liquid pushes up, while its weight and the string tension pull down. Find the volume of the cube, then the buoyant force and the mass of the cube, and finally solve the force balance for the tension.

steps.description: volume of the cube
steps.principle: Volume of a cube, V = a^3
steps.why: The cube is completely under the surface, so it displaces exactly its own volume of liquid. Both its weight and the buoyant force are proportional to this volume, so we need it first.

steps.description: buoyant force on the cube
steps.principle: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid, Fb = rho_l g V
steps.why: The cube is fully submerged, so the displaced liquid has the volume of the cube and the density of the liquid. This is the upward force the liquid exerts on the cube; it needs the volume but not the mass.

steps.description: mass of the cube
steps.principle: Definition of density, rho = m / V, so m = rho_s V
steps.why: The weight of the cube is its mass times g, and the problem gives its density instead of its mass; the density times the volume gives the mass.

steps.description: tension in the string
steps.principle: Newton's first law for a body in equilibrium: the net vertical force is zero, Fb = m g + T
steps.why: The cube is at rest, and the string is tied to the bottom of the tank, so it pulls the cube down along with its weight. The upward buoyant force must balance both, so the tension is the buoyant force minus the weight.

steps.text: Limiting case: if the density of the cube equalled that of the liquid, the buoyant force would equal the weight and the tension would be zero; the tension is positive only when the cube is less dense than the liquid, as it must be for a cube that needs to be held down. The result scales with the cube volume and with the density difference.

After the switch closes, the current in a series RL circuit rises exponentially toward its final value V/R with a time constant L over R. Find the time constant, the elapsed time in units of it, and then evaluate the rise law.

steps.description: time constant
steps.principle: The RL time constant: tau = L/R, the inductance divided by the series resistance
steps.why: Kirchhoff's loop rule for the circuit, V = I R + L dI/dt, has L/R as its only time scale, so it sets how quickly the current approaches its final value.

steps.description: elapsed time in units of the time constant
steps.principle: Dimensionless time: the elapsed time divided by the time constant, x = t/tau
steps.why: The current rise depends on time only through this ratio, so computing it first reduces the final step to evaluating an exponential.

steps.description: current in the circuit
steps.principle: The current rise in an RL circuit, solving V = I R + L dI/dt with I = 0 at t = 0: I = (V/R)(1 - e^(-t/tau))
steps.why: The coil opposes any sudden change of current, so the current starts at zero and grows toward the steady value V/R that Ohm's law would give if the coil were absent.

steps.text: At t = 0 the formula gives zero, at long times it tends to V/R, and the answer can never exceed V/R; at t = tau it reaches about 63 percent of V/R, which gives a quick order-of-magnitude test.
current in the circuit: 0.4661 A

This quantity has no path to the target: a resistor in series with the lamp lies in the lamp's own loop and shares no node with the coil's circuit, so the coil's current is fixed by the stated emf, resistance and inductance. Step 6. The RL time constant: tau = L/R, the inductance divided by the series resistance. Kirchhoff's loop rule for the circuit, V = I R + L dI/dt, has L/R as its only time scale, so it sets how quickly the current approaches its final value. tau = Lc/R  (SI units). tau = (0.2)/(20) = 0.01 (SI) = 0.01 s.

steps.principle: First law over one cycle, W = Qh - Qc, and the Clausius equality for a reversible cycle, Qc/Tc = Qh/Th (zero total entropy change)
steps.why: The engine returns to its initial state each cycle, so the work equals the heat taken in minus the heat rejected, and reversibility makes the rejected heat Qh Tc/Th. This gives W = Qh (1 - Tc/Th).

Step 1. Find the net work done in one cycle, in kJ.
Step 2. Given: Qh = 800 kJ (heat taken from the hot reservoir; given); Th = 600 K (temperature of the hot reservoir; given); Tc = 300 K (temperature of the cold reservoir; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The engine is reversible and operates in a cycle between the two reservoirs. The heat taken in is the heat taken from the hot reservoir in one cycle.
Step 4. The added sentence ("The apparatus was assembled on a sturdy wooden bench near the window.") contains no number: there is no quantity to use, so the problem is the base problem.
Step 5. Approach: For a reversible engine the second law fixes the ratio of the rejected heat to the absorbed heat through the reservoir temperatures, and the first law gives the net work as the difference of the two heats.
Step 6. First law over one cycle, W = Qh - Qc, and the Clausius equality for a reversible cycle, Qc/Tc = Qh/Th (zero total entropy change). The engine returns to its initial state each cycle, so the work equals the heat taken in minus the heat rejected, and reversibility makes the rejected heat Qh Tc/Th. This gives W = Qh (1 - Tc/Th). W = Qh*(1 - Tc/Th)  (SI units). W = (8e+05)*(1 - (300)/(600)) = 4e+05 (SI) = 400 kJ.
Step 7. Check: The work is always smaller than Qh and tends to zero as the cold temperature approaches the hot one. It would equal Qh only for a cold reservoir at absolute zero, so the efficiency 1 - Tc/Th must lie between zero and one.
Step 8. Answer: net work done in one cycle: 400 kJ.

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the energy stored in the coil, in mJ.
Step 2. Given: Lind = 250 mH (inductance of the coil; given); Icur = 3 A (steady current through the coil; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The coil is ideal: it has no resistance and no core losses. The current has reached its steady value.
Step 4. Approach: The energy in the magnetic field of an ideal coil depends only on its inductance and the steady current, so one application of the stored-energy formula, with the unit converted at the end, is enough.
Step 5. Energy stored in an inductor: U = (1/2) L I^2, the work done against the induced emf while the current is raised from zero to I (the integral of L i di). The coil is ideal and carries a steady current, so all the work done in building up the current is stored in its magnetic field, and the formula gives this energy directly. Wm = Lind*Icur**2/2  (SI units). Wm = (0.25)*(3)**2/2 = 1.125 (SI) = 1125 mJ.
Step 6. Check: The energy scales with the square of the current, so doubling the current must quadruple the answer; the unit is henry times ampere squared, which is a joule.
Step 7. Answer: energy stored in the coil: 1125 mJ.

steps.why: The time of flight found from the vertical motion is also the time during which the stone moves horizontally at the launch speed, so the product of the two is the horizontal distance travelled before landing.

steps.text: The distance grows with the launch speed and with the square root of the height, and it vanishes for a zero height. Step 2. Given: v = 15 m/s (horizontal launch speed of the stone; given); h = 20 m (height of the cliff edge above the ground; given); g = 9.8 m/s² (gravitational acceleration, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: g is a uniform constant of the stated value. Air resistance is neglected, so the horizontal velocity is constant. The ground is level and the stone is thrown exactly horizontally from the edge.
Step 4. Approach: The stone is a projectile, so its vertical and horizontal motions are independent. The vertical fall from the cliff edge fixes how long the stone is in the air; the constant horizontal speed over that time then gives the horizontal distance.
Step 5. Constant-acceleration kinematics for the vertical motion: the fall distance from rest is h = (1/2) g t^2. The stone is thrown horizontally, so it starts with zero vertical velocity and falls the height h with acceleration g; solving h = g t^2 / 2 for t gives the time to reach the ground, which does not depend on the horizontal speed. t = sqrt(2*h/g)  (SI units). t = sqrt(2*(20)/(9.8)) = 2.02 (SI) = 2.02 s.
Step 6. Uniform motion in the horizontal direction: with no horizontal force the horizontal velocity is constant, so distance = speed x time. The time of flight found from the vertical motion is also the time during which the stone moves horizontally at the launch speed, so the product of the two is the horizontal distance travelled before landing. dx = v*t  (SI units). dx = (15)*(2.02) = 30.3 (SI) = 30.3 m.
Step 7. Check: The distance grows with the launch speed and with the square root of the height, and it vanishes for a zero height. As a magnitude check, a fall of about 5 m takes about 1 s, so from such a height the stone lands roughly one second times its launch speed away; the units m/s times s give m.
Step 8. Answer: horizontal distance travelled by the stone: 30.3 m.

steps.text: The wall changes the momentum of the ball, so apply the impulse-momentum theorem along the line of motion: first the rebound speed from the coefficient of restitution, then the impulse as the change of momentum (the direction reverses), and finally the average force as the impulse divided by the contact time.

steps.description: speed of the ball just after it leaves the wall
steps.principle: Definition of the coefficient of restitution for a collision with a fixed wall: e = rebound speed / approach speed
steps.why: The wall does not move, so the ratio of the speeds after and before the impact is e; this gives the speed with which the ball leaves the wall, which is needed for the change of momentum.

steps.description: magnitude of the impulse given to the ball by the wall
steps.principle: Impulse-momentum theorem: the impulse J equals the change of momentum, J = m (v_final - v_initial)
steps.why: The ball reverses direction, so the velocity changes from +v to -vout and the magnitude of the change is v + vout, not their difference; multiplying by the mass gives the magnitude of the impulse. Gravity is negligible during the contact.

steps.description: magnitude of the average force of the wall on the ball
steps.principle: Definition of the average force: F_avg = J / (contact time), since the impulse is the time integral of the force
steps.why: The impulse is the area under the force-time curve, so dividing the impulse by the contact time gives the constant force that would deliver the same impulse, that is, the average force exerted by the wall.

steps.text: The answer must lie between m v / dt (a ball that stops dead, e = 0) and 2 m v / dt (a perfectly elastic bounce, e = 1). The units N s divided by s give N, and a lighter, slower ball or a longer contact gives a smaller force.

steps.description: speed of the ball just after it leaves the wall
steps.principle: Definition of the coefficient of restitution for a collision with a fixed wall: e = rebound speed / approach speed
steps.why: The wall does not move, so the ratio of the speeds after and before the impact is e; this gives the speed with which the ball leaves the wall, which is needed for the change of momentum.

steps.description: magnitude of the impulse given to the ball by the wall
steps.principle: Impulse-momentum theorem: the impulse J equals the change of momentum, J = m (v_final - v_initial)
steps.why: The ball reverses direction, so the velocity changes from +v to -vout and the magnitude of the change is v + vout, not their difference; multiplying by the mass gives the magnitude of the impulse. Gravity is negligible during the contact.

steps.principle: Definition of the average force: F_avg = J / (contact time), since the impulse is the time integral of the force

steps.text: A rolling sphere slows down on the way up because gravity pulls it down the slope while static friction also turns the spin down. Find the constant deceleration from the translational and rotational equations of motion with the rolling condition, then use constant-acceleration kinematics to find the distance at which the sphere stops.

steps.description: magnitude of the deceleration of the sphere along the incline
steps.principle: Newton's second law for the centre of mass (m a = m g sin(theta) - f), the rotational law (I alpha = f R with I = (2/5) m R^2) and the rolling condition a = alpha R
steps.why: Static friction f acts up the slope and the sphere rolls without slipping, so the rotational law gives f = (2/5) m a; substituting into the translational equation gives (7/5) a = g sin(theta). The sphere is therefore slowed at 5/7 of the rate of a frictionless sliding body.

steps.description: distance travelled up the incline before coming to rest
steps.principle: Constant-acceleration kinematics: v_final^2 = v0^2 - 2 a d with v_final = 0
steps.why: The deceleration is constant, and at the highest point of the motion the speed of the centre is zero; solving 0 = v0^2 - 2 a d for d gives the distance travelled along the incline.

steps.text: Energy check: the initial kinetic energy (1/2) m v0^2 (1 + 2/5) equals m g d sin(theta), giving the same d = 7 v0^2 / (10 g sin(theta)). The answer does not depend on the mass or the radius, and it is 7/5 times the distance that a frictionless sliding block would travel.
distance travelled up the incline: 6.085 m

A rolling sphere slows down on the way up because gravity pulls it down the slope while static friction also turns the spin down. Find the constant deceleration from the translational and rotational equations of motion with the rolling condition, then use constant-acceleration kinematics to find the distance at which the sphere stops.

steps.description: magnitude of the deceleration of the sphere along the incline
steps.principle: Newton's second law for the centre of mass (m a = m g sin(theta) - f), the rotational law (I alpha = f R with I = (2/5) m R^2) and the rolling condition a = alpha R
steps.why: Static friction f acts up the slope and the sphere rolls without slipping, so the rotational law gives f = (2/5) m a; substituting into the translational equation gives (7/5) a = g sin(theta). The sphere is therefore slowed at 5/7 of the rate of a frictionless sliding body.

steps.description: distance travelled up the incline before coming to rest
steps.principle: Constant-acceleration kinematics: v_final^2 = v0^2 - 2 a d with v_final = 0
steps.why: The deceleration is constant, and at the highest point of the motion the speed of the centre is zero; solving 0 = v0^2 - 2 a d for d gives the distance travelled along the incline.

items.description: radius of the Earth, a stated constant
items.name: R

items.description: gravitational acceleration at the surface of the Earth, a stated constant
items.name: g

items: The Earth is a uniform sphere of the stated radius, its rotation is neglected, and g is the stated value at its surface.

steps.text: Gravity supplies the centripetal force of a circular orbit. The surface gravity and the radius of the Earth give the product G M = g R^2, so no value of G is needed; find the orbital radius, then the orbital speed from Newton's second law, then the period as the circumference divided by the speed.

steps.description: radius of the orbit, measured from the centre of the Earth
steps.principle: Geometry: gravity depends on the distance from the centre of the Earth, so the orbital radius is r = R + h
steps.why: The altitude h is measured from the surface, while the law of gravitation uses the distance from the centre of the Earth, so the radius of the Earth must be added.

steps.description: orbital speed of the satellite
steps.principle: Newton's law of gravitation with Newton's second law for circular motion: G M m / r^2 = m v^2 / r, with G M = g R^2 from the surface gravity
steps.why: At the surface g = G M / R^2, so G M = g R^2 and the product G M is known; setting gravity equal to the centripetal force gives v = sqrt(G M / r) = sqrt(g R^2 / r), independent of the mass of the satellite.

steps.description: orbital period of the satellite
steps.principle: Uniform circular motion: period = circumference / speed, T = 2 pi r / v (equivalent to Kepler's third law)
steps.why: The satellite moves around a circle of length 2 pi r at the constant speed v, so the time for one orbit follows directly; the result is converted from seconds to minutes.

steps.text: For h = 0 the period is 2 pi sqrt(R / g), about 84 minutes, the shortest possible period around the Earth; the period grows as r to the power 3/2 (Kepler's third law). A satellite a few hundred kilometres up has a period of about 90 minutes.
orbital period of the satellite: 92.51 min

steps.text: The ladder is in static equilibrium, so the net force and the net torque on it are zero. Take torques about the foot to eliminate the unknown ground forces and find the force of the smooth wall; the vertical balance gives the normal force of the ground; the horizontal balance makes the friction equal to the wall force; the total ground force combines the two.

steps.description: horizontal force of the wall on the ladder
steps.principle: Condition of rotational equilibrium: the net torque about the foot of the ladder is zero
steps.why: The smooth wall pushes horizontally at the top with lever arm L sin(theta), the weight of the ladder acts at L/2 and that of the person at x L, with horizontal lever arms L cos(theta)/2 and x L cos(theta); the ground forces act at the foot and give no torque. So N_w L sin(theta) = (m/2 + M x) g L cos(theta), which gives N_w.

steps.description: vertical (normal) force of the ground on the ladder
steps.principle: Condition of translational equilibrium in the vertical direction: the normal force balances the total weight
steps.why: A smooth wall can exert no vertical force, so the normal force of the ground alone supports the weights of the ladder and the person, N_f = (m + M) g.

steps.description: magnitude of the total force of the ground on the ladder
steps.principle: Translational equilibrium in the horizontal direction (friction f = N_w) and vector addition of the perpendicular components, F = sqrt(f^2 + N_f^2)
steps.why: The ground exerts on the foot both the normal force and a horizontal friction force, which must cancel the wall force; the question asks for the magnitude of their resultant, found with the Pythagorean theorem.

steps.text: The resultant must exceed the total weight (m + M) g, because friction adds a horizontal part, and it tends to the total weight as the ladder becomes vertical (the wall force then tends to zero). The wall force rises as the person climbs higher.
total force of the ground on the ladder: 841.6 N

Step 2. Given: F0 = 80 mN (attractive force before contact; given); rq = 5 (ratio of the larger charge magnitude to the smaller; given); d0 = 30 cm (separation of the centres before contact; given); d1 = 60 cm (separation of the centres after contact; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The spheres are small compared with their separations, so each acts as a point charge, and nothing else disturbs the field. The spheres are identical conductors: on contact the total charge is shared equally and none leaks away. The force is the electrostatic force in air, taken as a vacuum.
Step 4. The added sentence ("Before the force was measured, the spheres were moved 26 cm further apart.") gives q = 26 cm. Moving the spheres q further apart makes the final separation d1 + q, and the force falls as 1 / (d1 + q)^2. In the graph this changes the input d1 (separation of the centres after contact): d1' = d1 + q = 60 + 26 = 86 cm. Every later step uses the changed d1.
Step 5. Approach: The charges are not given, but only their ratio and one force, so work with ratios and let the unknown constants cancel. First find the charge on each sphere after they touch, then use Coulomb's law to compare the new force with the old one, and finally scale the given force.
Step 6. Conservation of charge together with the symmetry of two identical conductors: on contact the total charge (q1 + q2) is divided equally, so each sphere gets (q1 + q2)/2. The charges have opposite signs, so with the smaller charge as the unit they are +1 and -(rq) and they partly cancel; each sphere is left with magnitude (rq - 1)/2 in these units, and both now have the same sign as the larger charge, so the force becomes repulsive. qshare = (rq - 1)/2  (SI units). qshare = ((5) - 1)/2 = 2 (SI) = 2.
Step 7. Coulomb's law: the force between point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation, F = k qa qb / r^2; the ratio of two states cancels k. Before contact the force is proportional to rq times 1 divided by d0 squared, and afterwards to qshare squared divided by d1 squared, so the ratio of new to old force is qshare squared over rq times (d0/d1) squared, with no need for k or the actual charges. Frel = qshare**2/rq*(d0/d1)**2  (SI units). Frel = (2)**2/(5)*((0.3)/(0.86))**2 = 0.09735 (SI) = 0.09735.
Step 8. Scaling by a ratio: the new force equals the given force times the force ratio just found. The old force was given, and the ratio converts it to the force after contact, which is the quantity asked for. F1 = F0*Frel  (SI units). F1 = (0.08)*(0.09735) = 0.007788 (SI) = 7.788 mN.
Step 9. Check: If the two charges were equal and opposite (rq = 1) they would cancel completely on contact and the formula gives zero force; if the spheres end up at the same separation as before, the force changes only by the charge factor qshare squared over rq, that is (rq - 1)^2/(4 rq), and it is smaller than the original force whenever that factor is below one.
Step 10. Answer: force between the spheres after contact: 7.788 mN.

steps.text: Find the additional charge supplied by the battery, in nC.

items: The slab has the same area as the plates and lies parallel to them; edge effects are neglected, so the capacitor is a stack of two layers in series.
The battery stays connected and is ideal, so the voltage across the capacitor is the emf before and after the insertion.
The slab is a linear dielectric of the stated constant, and the empty gap is a vacuum.

steps.text: With the battery connected the voltage is fixed, so the extra charge is the change of capacitance times the emf. Find the fraction of the gap that the slab fills, use it to get the new capacitance, and then multiply the change of capacitance by the emf.

steps.description: fraction of the gap filled by the slab
steps.principle: Geometry of the gap: the slab fills the fraction t/d of the plate separation d
steps.why: The slab has the same area as the plates, so only the thickness matters; the fraction tells how much of the gap is filled by dielectric and how much remains empty.

steps.description: capacitance with the slab inserted
steps.principle: The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is C = eps0 A / (gap), and a dielectric layer of constant kappa and thickness t counts as an air layer of thickness t/kappa; the empty layer and the dielectric layer are in series, so C = C0 / (1 - frac (1 - 1/kappa))
steps.why: The electric field is perpendicular to the plates and so to both layers, the same charge is on every layer, and the voltages of the two layers add; so the new capacitance follows from the empty capacitance and the fraction filled, without knowing the plate area or eps0.

steps.description: additional charge supplied by the battery
steps.principle: Definition of capacitance: Q = C V, so with the voltage held at the emf the charge changes by (C - C0) V
steps.why: The battery stays connected, so the voltage is the emf both before and after the insertion; the charge was C0 V and becomes C V, and the difference is the extra charge the battery supplies.

steps.text: If the slab fills the gap completely (frac = 1) the capacitance becomes kappa C0, and if there is no dielectric (kappa = 1) or no slab (frac = 0) it stays C0 and the extra charge is zero; the answer must be positive because the capacitance rises.

Step 3. Assumptions: The slab has the same area as the plates and lies parallel to them; edge effects are neglected, so the capacitor is a stack of two layers in series. The slab has the same area as the plates, so only the thickness matters; the fraction tells how much of the gap is filled by dielectric and how much remains empty. frac = t/d  (SI units). frac = (0.003)/(0.006) = 0.5 (SI) = 0.5.
Step 6. The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is C = eps0 A / (gap), and a dielectric layer of constant kappa and thickness t counts as an air layer of thickness t/kappa; the empty layer and the dielectric layer are in series, so C = C0 / (1 - frac (1 - 1/kappa)). steps.text: Find the radius of the circular path, in cm.

items.description: potential difference through which the bead is accelerated
items.name: V

items: The motion is non-relativistic and takes place in a vacuum; gravity and radiation are neglected.
The bead starts from rest and gains its speed only from the stated potential difference.
The magnetic field is uniform and perpendicular to the velocity of the bead on entry.

steps.text: First find the speed the bead gains in the accelerating potential difference, using energy conservation. The magnetic force then bends the path into a circle, so find the angular frequency of that motion and divide the speed by it to get the radius.

steps.description: speed of the bead on entering the field
steps.principle: Work-energy theorem for a charge in an electric field: the kinetic energy gained from rest equals the charge times the potential difference, (1/2) m v^2 = q V
steps.why: The bead starts from rest and the only force that does work is the electric force, because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and does no work; solving for v gives the speed on entering the field.

steps.description: cyclotron angular frequency of the bead
steps.principle: Newton's second law with the Lorentz force for a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field: q v B = m v^2/r, which means the charge circles with angular frequency omega = q B/m
steps.why: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and has constant size, so it acts as a pure centripetal force; the angular frequency of this circular motion does not depend on the speed and is set by the charge, the mass and the field.

steps.description: radius of the circular path
steps.principle: Circular motion: the speed equals the angular frequency times the radius, v = omega r, so r = v/omega
steps.why: Both the speed on entry and the angular frequency are known, and this relation gives the radius of the path that the question asks for, here converted to centimetres.

steps.text: The radius is r = m v/(q B), so it grows with the speed and falls as the field is increased, and it equals sqrt(2 m V/q)/B, which is the same expression with the speed eliminated; the units of r come out as metres.
radius of the circular path: 62.5 cm

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the radius of the circular path, in cm.
Step 2. Given: m = 0.1 g (mass of the bead; given); q = 2 mC (charge of the bead; given); V = 2.5 V (potential difference through which the bead is accelerated; given); B = 0.8 T (magnetic field strength; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The motion is non-relativistic and takes place in a vacuum; gravity and radiation are neglected. The bead starts from rest and gains its speed only from the stated potential difference. The magnetic field is uniform and perpendicular to the velocity of the bead on entry.
Step 4. Approach: First find the speed the bead gains in the accelerating potential difference, using energy conservation. The magnetic force then bends the path into a circle, so find the angular frequency of that motion and divide the speed by it to get the radius.
Step 5. Work-energy theorem for a charge in an electric field: the kinetic energy gained from rest equals the charge times the potential difference, (1/2) m v^2 = q V. The bead starts from rest and the only force that does work is the electric force, because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and does no work; solving for v gives the speed on entering the field. v = sqrt(2*q*V/m)  (SI units). v = sqrt(2*(0.002)*(2.5)/(0.0001)) = 10 (SI) = 10 m/s.
Step 6. Newton's second law with the Lorentz force for a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field: q v B = m v^2/r, which means the charge circles with angular frequency omega = q B/m. The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and has constant size, so it acts as a pure centripetal force; the angular frequency of this circular motion does not depend on the speed and is set by the charge, the mass and the field. wc = q*B/m  (SI units). wc = (0.002)*(0.8)/(0.0001) = 16 (SI) = 16 rad/s.
Step 7. Circular motion: the speed equals the angular frequency times the radius, v = omega r, so r = v/omega. Both the speed on entry and the angular frequency are known, and this relation gives the radius of the path that the question asks for, here converted to centimetres. r = v/wc  (SI units). r = (10)/(16) = 0.625 (SI) = 62.5 cm.
Step 8. Check: The radius is r = m v/(q B), so it grows with the speed and falls as the field is increased, and it equals sqrt(2 m V/q)/B, which is the same expression with the speed eliminated; the units of r come out as metres.
Step 9. Answer: radius of the circular path: 62.5 cm.

steps.text: The rod speeds up until the magnetic braking force along the rails balances the pull of gravity along the rails. Find the component of the field that matters for the loop, resolve the weight along the incline, and then set up the force balance with the induced emf and current to solve for the speed.

steps.description: component of the field perpendicular to the plane of the rails
steps.principle: Magnetic flux through a loop is Phi = B A cos(angle between B and the normal to the loop), so only the component of the vertical field normal to the plane of the rails, B cos(theta), changes the flux
steps.why: The field is vertical but the loop lies in the sloping plane, so the effective field for the flux and for the force along the slope is B cos(theta); the same factor enters the induced emf and the force component along the rails.

steps.description: component of the weight along the rails
steps.principle: Resolution of the weight on an incline: the component of the weight m g along the slope is m g sin(theta)
steps.why: Only this component accelerates the rod down the rails, so at the terminal speed it is the force that the magnetic braking force along the rails has to balance.

steps.description: terminal speed of the rod
steps.principle: Faraday's law, emf = B_eff ell v, Ohm's law, I = emf/R, and the magnetic force on the rod, F = B_eff I ell along the slope, together with force balance at constant speed: Fg = B_eff^2 ell^2 v/R, so v = Fg R/(B_eff ell)^2
steps.why: As the rod moves, the area of the loop changes and an emf is induced; the resulting current feels a force that opposes the motion (Lenz's law) and grows with speed, so the speed levels off where this force equals the component of the weight along the slope.

steps.text: At the terminal speed the power supplied by gravity, Fg v, must equal the power dissipated in the resistor, (B_eff ell v)^2/R, which is the same equation; a larger resistance (less braking current) must give a higher terminal speed, and a flat track (theta = 0) gives zero speed.
terminal speed of the rod: 2.836 m/s

steps.text: Find the average power dissipated in the load, in W.

items.description: ratio of primary turns to secondary turns
items.name: a

items: The transformer is ideal: perfect coupling, no losses and negligible magnetising current.
All emfs and currents are rms values, the load is purely resistive and the generator is a sinusoidal source in series with its internal resistance.

steps.text: An ideal transformer makes the load look like a resistor of a_squared times RL in the primary circuit, which is in series with the generator's internal resistance. Find this reflected resistance, the primary current from the series loop, convert it to the secondary current with the turns ratio, and then the power in the load.

steps.description: load resistance as seen from the primary side
steps.principle: Impedance reflection by an ideal transformer: with V2 = V1/a and I2 = a I1, the resistance seen at the primary is V1/I1 = a^2 V2/I2 = a^2 R_L
steps.why: The primary circuit contains the generator and the transformer, so the whole secondary circuit can be replaced by one resistor a squared times the load resistance connected across the primary, which turns the problem into a simple series circuit.

steps.description: rms current in the primary circuit
steps.principle: Ohm's law for the series loop of the generator: the rms current equals the emf divided by the total resistance, I = Vs/(Rs + Rref)
steps.why: The generator's internal resistance and the reflected load resistance are in series with the same current, so the primary current follows from the emf and the sum of the two resistances.

steps.description: rms current in the load
steps.principle: Ideal transformer current relation: the ampere-turns are equal, N1 I1 = N2 I2, so I2 = a I1 with a = N1/N2
steps.why: With more turns on the primary than on the secondary the current is stepped up in the secondary, and this gives the rms current that flows through the load.

steps.description: average power dissipated in the load
steps.principle: Joule heating in a resistor: the average power is P = I_rms^2 R
steps.why: The load is purely resistive and the currents are rms values, so the average power dissipated in the load is the square of its rms current times its resistance.

steps.text: The power taken from the generator, I1^2 (Rs + Rref), minus the power lost in the internal resistance, I1^2 Rs, must equal the load power I2^2 RL, because the ideal transformer dissipates nothing; with Rs = 0 the load power would be Vs^2/(a^2 RL).
average power dissipated in the load: 45 W

steps.text: Find the frequency of the damped oscillation, in Hz.

items: The resistor, coil and capacitor are ideal and in series; any resistance of the coil is included in the stated resistance, and there is no source.
The circuit is underdamped: the resistance is small enough that the charge oscillates.

steps.text: For a series RLC circuit without a source the charge obeys a damped oscillator equation. Compute the damping rate and the undamped angular frequency, combine them into the damped angular frequency, and convert it to a frequency in hertz.

steps.description: damping rate R/(2L)
steps.principle: Kirchhoff's loop rule for the series circuit, L q'' + R q' + q/C = 0, which has the damping form with alpha = R/(2L) as the decay rate of the amplitude
steps.why: Dividing the loop equation by L puts it in the standard damped-oscillator form, and the term with the first derivative then defines the damping rate R/(2L), which is how fast the amplitude falls as e^(-alpha t).

steps.description: undamped angular frequency
steps.principle: The undamped LC oscillation has angular frequency omega0 = 1/sqrt(L C), from the same equation with R = 0
steps.why: The coil and capacitor alone would exchange energy at this angular frequency, and it is the restoring term in the damped equation, so it is needed for the next step.

steps.description: damped angular frequency
steps.principle: Solution of the damped oscillator: q is proportional to e^(-alpha t) cos(omega_d t) with omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - alpha^2) when alpha < omega0
steps.why: Trying exponential solutions e^(s t) in the loop equation gives s = -alpha plus or minus i omega_d; the imaginary part is the angular frequency of the oscillation, which is lower than omega0 because of the damping.

steps.description: frequency of the damped oscillation
steps.principle: Relation between frequency and angular frequency: f = omega/(2 pi)
steps.why: The question asks for a frequency in hertz and the previous step gave an angular frequency in radians per second, so dividing by two pi gives the number of oscillations per second.

steps.text: With R = 0 the formula must reduce to the LC frequency 1/(2 pi sqrt(L C)), and the damped frequency must always be smaller than that; the oscillation exists only while alpha is smaller than omega0, which holds for the stated values.
frequency of the damped oscillation: 63.66 Hz

Step 3. Assumptions: The resistor, coil and capacitor are ideal and in series; any resistance of the coil is included in the stated resistance, and there is no source. The circuit is underdamped: the resistance is small enough that the charge oscillates.

items: The resistor, coil and capacitor are ideal and in series; any resistance of the coil is included in the stated resistance, and there is no source.
The circuit is underdamped: the resistance is small enough that the charge oscillates.

steps.text: The added sentence ("A 19 μF capacitor is connected in parallel with the capacitor of this circuit.") gives q = 19 μF. A capacitor in parallel with the capacitor adds to its capacitance, so the capacitance of the loop becomes C + q; the circuit stays underdamped for every study value. In the graph this changes the input C (capacitance of the capacitor): C' = C + q = 40 + 19 = 59 μF. Every later step uses the changed C.

For a series RLC circuit without a source the charge obeys a damped oscillator equation. Compute the damping rate and the undamped angular frequency, combine them into the damped angular frequency, and convert it to a frequency in hertz.

steps.description: damping rate R/(2L)
steps.principle: Kirchhoff's loop rule for the series circuit, L q'' + R q' + q/C = 0, which has the damping form with alpha = R/(2L) as the decay rate of the amplitude
steps.why: Dividing the loop equation by L puts it in the standard damped-oscillator form, and the term with the first derivative then defines the damping rate R/(2L), which is how fast the amplitude falls as e^(-alpha t).

steps.description: undamped angular frequency
steps.principle: The undamped LC oscillation has angular frequency omega0 = 1/sqrt(L C), from the same equation with R = 0
steps.why: The coil and capacitor alone would exchange energy at this angular frequency, and it is the restoring term in the damped equation, so it is needed for the next step.

steps.description: damped angular frequency
steps.principle: Solution of the damped oscillator: q is proportional to e^(-alpha t) cos(omega_d t) with omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - alpha^2) when alpha < omega0
steps.why: Trying exponential solutions e^(s t) in the loop equation gives s = -alpha plus or minus i omega_d; the imaginary part is the angular frequency of the oscillation, which is lower than omega0 because of the damping.

steps.description: frequency of the damped oscillation
steps.principle: Relation between frequency and angular frequency: f = omega/(2 pi)
steps.why: The question asks for a frequency in hertz and the previous step gave an angular frequency in radians per second, so dividing by two pi gives the number of oscillations per second.

steps.text: With R = 0 the formula must reduce to the LC frequency 1/(2 pi sqrt(L C)), and the damped frequency must always be smaller than that; the oscillation exists only while alpha is smaller than omega0, which holds for the stated values.
frequency of the damped oscillation: 44.87 Hz

steps.text: We are asked for the work done on a gas that is compressed slowly with no heat exchange. First find the final temperature from the adiabatic law for an ideal gas, then use the first law of thermodynamics with zero heat: the work done on the gas equals the increase of its internal energy.

steps.description: final temperature of the gas
steps.principle: Reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas: T V^(gamma - 1) is constant, equivalently p V^gamma is constant
steps.why: The compression is slow (quasi-static) and no heat flows, so the gas moves along an adiabat. With the compression ratio r = V1/V2 the law gives T2 = T1 r^(gamma - 1), which tells us how hot the gas becomes.

steps.description: work done on the gas
steps.principle: First law of thermodynamics, delta U = Q + W_on with Q = 0, and delta U = n Cv delta T for an ideal gas, with Cv = R/(gamma - 1) from gamma = Cp/Cv and Mayer's relation Cp - Cv = R
steps.why: No heat is exchanged, so all the work done on the gas goes into internal energy. Writing Cv through gamma and R lets us compute the work from the temperature rise already found: W = n R (T2 - T1)/(gamma - 1).

steps.text: The work is positive because compressing a gas adiabatically heats it. It tends to zero as r tends to 1, and it exceeds the work of an isothermal compression to the same volume, n R T1 ln r, because the hotter gas pushes back harder.
work done on the gas: 4.045 kJ

steps.description: thermal resistance of the brick layer

steps.description: thermal resistance of the foam layer
steps.principle: Fourier's law of heat conduction, with thermal resistance R = L/(k A)

steps.description: rate of heat flow through the wall
steps.principle: Thermal resistances in series add (steady heat current is continuous), and the heat current is P = delta T / R_total, the thermal analogue of Ohm's law
steps.why: In steady state no heat accumulates at the interface, so the same P flows through both layers and the temperature drops across them add up to the given difference between the outer surfaces.

steps.text: The heat current must be smaller than the current through either layer alone with the full temperature difference, dT/R1 or dT/R2, and the layer with the larger resistance takes the larger share of the temperature drop. Doubling the temperature difference doubles the heat current.

Step 3. Assumptions: The engine is reversible, runs in whole cycles and rejects its waste heat to the lake. The lake is so large that its temperature stays constant, and the tank loses no heat except through the engine. The specific heat capacity of water is the stated constant, and the water stays liquid.
Step 4. The added sentence ("The apparatus was assembled on a sturdy wooden bench near the window.") contains no number: there is no quantity to use, so the problem is the base problem.
Step 5. Approach: The engine works between a finite body that cools down and a large lake. Its maximum work is the heat given up by the water minus the heat that must be rejected to the lake, and the second law fixes the rejected heat for a reversible engine through the entropy that the water loses. We find the heat, the entropy change, then the work.
Step 6. Specific heat relation Q = m c delta T for the water cooling from Tb to the lake temperature Tl. This is the total heat that the water gives up to the engine as it cools to the lake temperature, which is the energy input of the engine over the whole process. Q = m*c*(Tb - Tl)  (SI units). Q = (2)*(4186)*((360) - (290)) = 5.86e+05 (SI) = 586 kJ.
Step 7. Entropy change for heat exchanged reversibly, dS = dQ/T with dQ = m c dT, so the entropy decrease is m c ln(Tb/Tl). The temperature of the water changes continuously, so the entropy lost by the water is found by integrating dQ/T. A reversible engine produces no entropy, so this loss is exactly the entropy gained by the lake. dS = m*c*log(Tb/Tl)  (SI units). dS = (2)*(4186)*log((360)/(290)) = 1810 (SI) = 1810 J/K.
Step 8. First law for the engine (work = heat taken in minus heat rejected) and second law for a reversible engine (total entropy change zero): the rejected heat is Tl times the entropy decrease of the water, so W = Q - Tl dS. The lake receives the rejected heat at its constant temperature Tl, so the rejected heat is Tl times the entropy it gains, which equals dS; subtracting it from Q gives the largest possible work. W = Q - Tl*dS  (SI units). W = (5.86e+05) - (290)*(1810) = 6.108e+04 (SI) = 61.08 kJ.
Step 9. Check: The work is positive and smaller than Q, and it is smaller than Q times the Carnot efficiency 1 - Tl/Tb of the initial temperature, because the water gets colder as heat is drawn from it. As Tb approaches Tl the work tends to zero faster than Q does.

steps.text: The resonant frequency of a pipe is the speed of sound divided by the wavelength of the standing wave. We find the speed of sound in the gas from its temperature and molar mass, find the wavelength of the second-lowest standing wave that the closed-open boundary conditions allow, and divide.

steps.description: speed of sound in the gas
steps.principle: Speed of sound in an ideal gas for adiabatic compressions: c = sqrt(gamma R T / M), which follows from c squared = gamma p / rho and the ideal-gas law p = rho R T / M
steps.why: The wave speed is needed to convert a wavelength into a frequency. The gas is ideal and sound is adiabatic, so the speed depends only on the ratio of specific heats, the temperature and the molar mass (in kilograms per mole).

steps.description: wavelength of the second-lowest resonance
steps.principle: Standing waves in a pipe closed at one end and open at the other: a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end require L = (2k - 1) lam / 4, so the resonances are the odd quarter-wavelength fits
steps.why: The lowest resonance has L = lam/4 and the second-lowest has L = 3 lam/4, so the wavelength of the second-lowest resonance is four thirds of the pipe length.

steps.description: frequency of the second-lowest resonance
steps.principle: The wave relation for a periodic wave: speed = frequency times wavelength
steps.why: We have the wave speed in the gas and the wavelength of the standing wave, so their ratio is the resonant frequency asked for.

Step 2. Given: gam = 1.4 (ratio of the specific heats of the gas; given); M = 29 g/mol (molar mass of the gas; given); T = 293 K (temperature of the gas; given); L = 0.6 m (length of the pipe; given); R = 8.314 J/(mol*K) (molar gas constant, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The gas is ideal and sound travels through it adiabatically. The molar gas constant is the stated constant. The pipe is closed at one end and open at the other, its width is much smaller than its length, and end corrections are neglected.
Step 4. The added sentence ("Before the resonances are measured, a heater warms the gas in the pipe by 45 K.") gives q = 45 K. Warming the gas in the pipe by q before the resonances are measured gives it the temperature T + q; the speed of sound depends on that temperature. In the graph this changes the input T (temperature of the gas): T' = T + q = 293 + 45 = 338 K. Every later step uses the changed T.
Step 5. Approach: The resonant frequency of a pipe is the speed of sound divided by the wavelength of the standing wave. We find the speed of sound in the gas from its temperature and molar mass, find the wavelength of the second-lowest standing wave that the closed-open boundary conditions allow, and divide.
Step 6. Speed of sound in an ideal gas for adiabatic compressions: c = sqrt(gamma R T / M), which follows from c squared = gamma p / rho and the ideal-gas law p = rho R T / M. The wave speed is needed to convert a wavelength into a frequency. The gas is ideal and sound is adiabatic, so the speed depends only on the ratio of specific heats, the temperature and the molar mass (in kilograms per mole). c = sqrt(gam*R*T/M)  (SI units). c = sqrt((1.4)*(8.314)*(338)/(0.029)) = 368.3 (SI) = 368.3 m/s.
Step 7. Standing waves in a pipe closed at one end and open at the other: a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end require L = (2k - 1) lam / 4, so the resonances are the odd quarter-wavelength fits. The lowest resonance has L = lam/4 and the second-lowest has L = 3 lam/4, so the wavelength of the second-lowest resonance is four thirds of the pipe length. lam = 4*L/3  (SI units). lam = 4*(0.6)/3 = 0.8 (SI) = 0.8 m.
Step 8. The wave relation for a periodic wave: speed = frequency times wavelength. We have the wave speed in the gas and the wavelength of the standing wave, so their ratio is the resonant frequency asked for. f = c/lam  (SI units). f = (368.3)/(0.8) = 460.4 (SI) = 460.4 Hz.
Step 9. Check: The second-lowest resonance of a closed pipe is three times the fundamental, c/(4L), so the answer must equal 3c/(4L). The speed of sound is a few hundred metres per second for heavy gases and air and about a thousand for a light gas such as helium, so frequencies of order a hundred hertz to a few kilohertz are reasonable for a pipe of this length.
Step 10. Answer: second-lowest resonant frequency of the gas column: 460.4 Hz.

items: The refractive index of the air is the stated constant.
The fibre is straight and has a core of uniform refractive index surrounded by a cladding of lower uniform refractive index.
The ray travels in a plane that contains the axis of the fibre, and the end face is flat and perpendicular to the axis.

steps.text: The added sentence ("For an earlier experiment only, the end of the fibre was held in a liquid instead of in the air; the refractive index of the liquid is 1.33.") gives 1.33 1. This quantity has no path to the target: the fibre end was dipped into the liquid for an earlier experiment only, which is over; in the stated experiment the rays enter from the stated air. It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.

A ray is guided when it strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle of incidence at least equal to the critical angle. The steepest guided ray inside the core is found from the critical angle, and Snell's law at the end face then gives the largest angle in air from which such a ray can enter.

steps.description: critical angle at the core-cladding boundary
steps.principle: Total internal reflection and the critical angle: at the core-cladding boundary Snell's law with a refraction angle of ninety degrees gives sin(theta_c) = n2 / n1
steps.why: A ray is trapped only if its angle of incidence on the boundary is at least the critical angle, so the critical angle sets the limiting ray that is still guided.

steps.description: largest angle between a guided ray and the axis, inside the core
steps.principle: Geometry of the straight fibre: the normal to the core-cladding boundary is perpendicular to the axis, so a ray whose angle of incidence on the boundary is theta_c makes the angle (ninety degrees minus theta_c) with the axis
steps.why: This converts the limiting angle at the side wall into the angle that the limiting ray makes with the axis inside the core, which is also its angle of refraction at the end face because the end-face normal lies along the axis.

steps.description: largest angle of incidence on the fibre end, measured from the axis, for a guided ray
steps.principle: Snell's law of refraction at the end face: n0 sin(theta) = n1 sin(theta_r), with both angles measured from the axis, which is the normal to the end face
steps.why: The limiting ray inside the core came from the largest entry angle, so solving for theta gives the largest angle in air that is still guided; this is the acceptance angle asked for.

steps.text: Combining the steps gives n0 sin(theta_max) = sqrt(n1 squared - n2 squared), the numerical aperture of the fibre. If the cladding index approached the core index, the acceptance angle would shrink to zero, and the sine of the angle must stay below one, which it does for these indices.
largest angle of acceptance: 24.83 deg

It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.
Step 5. Approach: A ray is guided when it strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle of incidence at least equal to the critical angle. The steepest guided ray inside the core is found from the critical angle, and Snell's law at the end face then gives the largest angle in air from which such a ray can enter.
Step 6. Total internal reflection and the critical angle: at the core-cladding boundary Snell's law with a refraction angle of ninety degrees gives sin(theta_c) = n2 / n1. A ray is trapped only if its angle of incidence on the boundary is at least the critical angle, so the critical angle sets the limiting ray that is still guided. thc = asin(n2/n1)  (SI units). thc = asin((1.44)/(1.5)) = 1.287 (SI) = 73.74 deg.

steps.description: critical angle at the core-cladding boundary

steps.description: largest angle between a guided ray and the axis, inside the core

steps.description: diffraction angle of the shorter wavelength
steps.principle: The grating equation for a plane grating at normal incidence: the maxima lie where the path difference between neighbouring slits, d sin(theta), equals a whole number m of wavelengths

steps.principle: The grating equation again, d sin(theta) = m lam, now with the longer wavelength
steps.why: The same slit spacing and order apply, so the longer wavelength is diffracted to theta = asin(m lam2 / d), farther from the central beam than the shorter one.

steps.principle: Definition of the angular separation of two maxima on the same side of the central beam as the difference of their angles
steps.why: Both maxima lie on the same side of the undeviated beam, so subtracting the smaller angle from the larger gives the separation the question asks for.

Step 2. Given: d = 4 μm (spacing between neighbouring slits of the grating; given); lam1 = 450 nm (shorter wavelength in the beam; given); lam2 = 650 nm (longer wavelength in the beam; given); m = 2 (order of the diffraction maxima that are compared; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The grating is a plane transmission grating with equally spaced narrow slits, and the beam is collimated and falls on it at normal incidence. Both maxima are on the same side of the undeviated central beam, which is the order zero maximum. Each wavelength has its own sharp maximum of the stated order.
Step 4. The added sentence ("For this measurement, light of 490 nm wavelength replaced the shorter wavelength in the beam.") gives q = 490 nm. Light of wavelength q replaces the shorter wavelength of the beam, so lam1 becomes q and the separation is measured between q and the longer wavelength. In the graph this changes the input lam1 (shorter wavelength in the beam): lam1' = q = 490 nm (was 450 nm). Every later step uses the changed lam1.
Step 5. Approach: Each wavelength has its own diffraction angle in a given order, given by the grating equation. We find the angle for each of the two wavelengths in the stated order and subtract.
Step 6. The grating equation for a plane grating at normal incidence: the maxima lie where the path difference between neighbouring slits, d sin(theta), equals a whole number m of wavelengths. The slit spacing and the order are given, so the shorter wavelength has its maximum of that order at theta = asin(m lam1 / d), with the sine less than one so that the order exists. th1 = asin(m*lam1/d)  (SI units). th1 = asin((2)*(4.9e-07)/(4e-06)) = 0.2475 (SI) = 14.18 deg.
Step 7. The grating equation again, d sin(theta) = m lam, now with the longer wavelength. The same slit spacing and order apply, so the longer wavelength is diffracted to theta = asin(m lam2 / d), farther from the central beam than the shorter one. th2 = asin(m*lam2/d)  (SI units). th2 = asin((2)*(6.5e-07)/(4e-06)) = 0.331 (SI) = 18.97 deg.
Step 8. Definition of the angular separation of two maxima on the same side of the central beam as the difference of their angles. Both maxima lie on the same side of the undeviated beam, so subtracting the smaller angle from the larger gives the separation the question asks for. dth = th2 - th1  (SI units). dth = (0.331) - (0.2475) = 0.08349 (SI) = 4.784 deg.
Step 9. Check: The longer wavelength must be diffracted through the larger angle, so the separation is positive. For small angles it is about m (lam2 - lam1) / d, so a coarser grating (a larger spacing) would separate the lines less, and the true separation is a little larger than this estimate because of the asin.

steps.text: Some power is reflected at each of the two surfaces of the plate, and the light trapped between the surfaces bounces back and forth, adding a little to the transmitted power on every round trip. We find the reflectance of one surface, sum the whole series of transmitted beams, and multiply by the incident power.

steps.description: fraction of the power reflected at a single surface
steps.principle: The Fresnel reflectance at normal incidence, R = ((n - na) / (n + na)) squared, which follows from continuity of the tangential electric and magnetic fields at an interface
steps.why: Both surfaces of the plate are air-glass interfaces and the beam is at normal incidence, so each surface reflects the same fraction R of the power that reaches it, from whichever side it arrives.

steps.description: fraction of the power transmitted by the whole plate
steps.principle: Incoherent multiple reflections in a lossless plate: the first transmitted beam carries (1 - R) squared, each round trip inside multiplies by R squared, and the series (1 - R) squared (1 + R squared + R to the fourth + ...) sums to (1 - R) / (1 + R)
steps.why: The powers of the beams add because they do not interfere, and no light is absorbed, so the geometric series of transmitted beams gives the fraction of the incident power that the plate transmits in total.

steps.description: power of the transmitted beam
steps.principle: Definition of the transmitted fraction: the transmitted power equals the transmittance times the incident power
steps.why: The beam power is given and the fraction transmitted by the plate is known, so their product is the transmitted power asked for.

steps.text: If the glass index equalled the air index there would be no reflection and all of the power would be transmitted. The total reflected fraction is 2R/(1+R), and the transmitted fraction plus this must equal one (no absorption); the transmitted fraction exceeds the single-pass value (1 - R) squared because of the extra beams, and it is less than one.

Step 2. Given: na = 1 (refractive index of the air around the plate, a stated constant; stated constant); n = 1.5 (refractive index of the glass; given); P0 = 50 mW (power of the incident beam; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The refractive index of the air is the stated constant. The plate is parallel-sided and does not absorb light, and the beams reflected inside it do not interfere, so that their powers add. The beam falls at normal incidence and the reflectance of each surface is given by the Fresnel formula for normal incidence.
Step 4. Approach: Some power is reflected at each of the two surfaces of the plate, and the light trapped between the surfaces bounces back and forth, adding a little to the transmitted power on every round trip. We find the reflectance of one surface, sum the whole series of transmitted beams, and multiply by the incident power.
Step 5. The Fresnel reflectance at normal incidence, R = ((n - na) / (n + na)) squared, which follows from continuity of the tangential electric and magnetic fields at an interface. Both surfaces of the plate are air-glass interfaces and the beam is at normal incidence, so each surface reflects the same fraction R of the power that reaches it, from whichever side it arrives. Rf = ((n - na)/(n + na))**2  (SI units). Rf = (((1.5) - (1))/((1.5) + (1)))**2 = 0.04 (SI) = 0.04.
Step 6. Incoherent multiple reflections in a lossless plate: the first transmitted beam carries (1 - R) squared, each round trip inside multiplies by R squared, and the series (1 - R) squared (1 + R squared + R to the fourth + ...) sums to (1 - R) / (1 + R). The powers of the beams add because they do not interfere, and no light is absorbed, so the geometric series of transmitted beams gives the fraction of the incident power that the plate transmits in total. Tf = (1 - Rf)/(1 + Rf)  (SI units). Tf = (1 - (0.04))/(1 + (0.04)) = 0.9231 (SI) = 0.9231.
Step 7. Definition of the transmitted fraction: the transmitted power equals the transmittance times the incident power. The beam power is given and the fraction transmitted by the plate is known, so their product is the transmitted power asked for. Pt = Tf*P0  (SI units). Pt = (0.9231)*(0.05) = 0.04615 (SI) = 46.15 mW.
Step 8. Check: If the glass index equalled the air index there would be no reflection and all of the power would be transmitted. The total reflected fraction is 2R/(1+R), and the transmitted fraction plus this must equal one (no absorption); the transmitted fraction exceeds the single-pass value (1 - R) squared because of the extra beams, and it is less than one.
Step 9. Answer: total transmitted power: 46.15 mW.

items.name: hc

items.name: mc2
