items: The constant hc has the stated value and is used for every photon energy and wavelength.
The electron rest energy has the stated value.
The speed of light has the stated value.
Each electron absorbs one photon, and the fastest electrons lose no energy besides the work function.
The electron speed is far below c, so the non-relativistic kinetic energy applies.

steps.text: The question asks for the speed of the fastest photoelectrons. Work in energy units: get the photon energy from the wavelength, subtract the work function (Einstein's photoelectric equation) to obtain the maximum kinetic energy, and only then convert that kinetic energy into a speed with the non-relativistic relation.

steps.description: energy of one photon of the light
steps.principle: Planck-Einstein relation: a photon of wavelength lambda carries the energy E = h c / lambda.
steps.why: Light interacts with the electrons in the metal one photon at a time, so the energy a single electron can receive is the energy of one photon, which the stated product hc and the wavelength give directly.

steps.description: maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron
steps.principle: Einstein's photoelectric equation: K_max = E_photon - phi, which is conservation of energy for one photon absorbed by one electron.
steps.why: The most energetic electrons come from the surface and lose only the minimum energy phi needed to escape the metal, so all the rest of the photon energy remains as their kinetic energy.

steps.description: speed of the fastest photoelectrons
steps.principle: Non-relativistic kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v^2, so v = c sqrt(2 K / (m c^2)) when the mass is written through the rest energy m c^2.
steps.why: The kinetic energy is only a few electronvolts, tiny compared with the electron rest energy, so the classical relation is accurate, and using the rest energy over c squared as the mass lets us use the stated constants.

steps.text: At the threshold, where the photon energy equals the work function, K_max and v vanish, and below it no electron is emitted. A kinetic energy of a few electronvolts against a rest energy of hundreds of keV gives v/c of a few thousandths, which confirms that the non-relativistic treatment is justified.
speed of the fastest photoelectrons: 968 km/s

steps.why: The wave function must vanish at both walls, which fits n half-wavelengths into the width L, so the allowed momenta and hence the energies are quantised; E_1 is the unit in which all the levels of this well are measured.

steps.description: energy difference between the two levels
steps.principle: Level spectrum E_n = n^2 E_1 and conservation of energy: the photon takes the energy difference E_i - E_f = (n_i^2 - n_f^2) E_1.
steps.why: The electron goes from a higher to a lower level and the energy it loses is carried away by one photon, the recoil of the walls being negligible, so this difference is the photon energy.

steps.description: wavelength of the emitted photon
steps.principle: Planck-Einstein relation E = h c / lambda, so lambda = h c / E.
steps.why: The photon energy is now known, and the stated product hc converts it directly into the wavelength of the light.

steps.text: The ground-state energy scales as 1/L^2, so a wider well has closer levels and a longer photon wavelength, lambda proportional to L^2. Dimensionally (J m)^2 / (J m^2) is an energy. items: The electron rest energy has the stated value.
The constant hbar c has the stated value.
The barrier is rectangular with the stated height and the electron arrives from one side with the stated kinetic energy.
The transmission probability is given by the exponential approximation T = exp(-2 kappa a) for a wide barrier, with kappa = sqrt(2 m (U0 - E)) / hbar.

steps.text: The question asks for the width of the barrier for which the stated approximate transmission probability has the given value. Find how far the barrier top lies above the electron's energy, then the decay constant of the wave inside the barrier, and then invert T = exp(-2 kappa a) for the width.

steps.description: amount by which the barrier exceeds the electron energy
steps.principle: Classically forbidden region: the electron's kinetic energy lies below the barrier top by U0 - E.
steps.why: Inside the barrier the wave function does not oscillate but decays, and the rate of decay is set by how much the barrier exceeds the electron energy.

steps.description: decay constant of the wave function inside the barrier
steps.principle: Time-independent Schroedinger equation inside a constant potential above the energy: psi proportional to exp(-kappa x) with kappa = sqrt(2 m (U0 - E)) / hbar = sqrt(2 (m c^2) (U0 - E)) / (hbar c).
steps.why: The decay constant kappa controls how quickly the probability falls across the barrier, and the stated rest energy and hbar c let us compute it from the energy deficit.

steps.description: barrier width
steps.principle: Exponential (thick-barrier) approximation for tunnelling: T = exp(-2 kappa a), so a = -ln(T) / (2 kappa).
steps.why: The stated transmission probability is a known number, so taking the natural logarithm of the exponential approximation and solving for a gives the barrier width.

steps.text: A wider barrier or a larger deficit gives a smaller transmission, so a falls as kappa rises and grows as the required T gets smaller. If T tended to one the width would tend to zero. A deficit of a few electronvolts gives kappa of several per nanometre, so widths of a fraction of a nanometre are the expected order of magnitude.

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the photon energy at the spectral peak of the second star, in eV.
Step 2. Given: lam1 = 500 nm (peak wavelength of the spectrum of the first star; given); T1 = 5800 K (surface temperature of the first star; given); T2 = 2900 K (surface temperature of the second star; given); hc = 1240 eV*nm (product of the Planck constant and the speed of light, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: Both stars radiate as ideal blackbodies, and the peak is the maximum of the spectral radiance per unit wavelength. The product hc is the stated constant.
Step 4. Approach: The peak wavelength of a blackbody spectrum scales inversely with temperature, so we first get the peak wavelength of the second star from the data of the first star, and then convert that wavelength to a photon energy.
Step 5. Wien's displacement law: the wavelength of maximum spectral radiance of a blackbody is inversely proportional to its temperature, lambda_max times T = constant. Both stars are blackbodies, so the product of peak wavelength and temperature has the same value for both; the known pair of the first star fixes it, which gives the peak wavelength of the second star without needing the value of Wien's constant. lam2 = lam1*T1/T2  (SI units). lam2 = (5e-07)*(5800)/(2900) = 1e-06 (SI) = 1000 nm.
Step 6. Planck-Einstein relation for a photon: E = h f = h c / lambda. The question asks for the energy of a photon at the peak wavelength of the second star; with hc given in eV nm and the wavelength in nm, the energy comes out directly in eV. Eph = hc/lam2  (SI units). Eph = (1.987e-25)/(1e-06) = 1.987e-19 (SI) = 1.24 eV.
Step 7. Check: The hotter a star the shorter its peak wavelength and the larger the photon energy at the peak, so the sign of the change between the two stars must agree with the temperature ratio. The product of the photon energy in eV and the wavelength in nm must reproduce the stated value of hc.
Step 8. Answer: photon energy at the spectral peak of the second star: 1.24 eV.

steps.text: The Venturi meter converts a flow rate into a pressure difference between the wide section and the throat, and the U-tube measures that difference. Work backwards: first get the pressure difference from the manometer reading, then use continuity and Bernoulli's equation to find the speed in the wide section, then multiply by the area for the flow rate.

steps.description: pressure difference between the wide section and the throat
steps.principle: Hydrostatic pressure law applied to the U-tube: the pressure difference between two tappings equals the weight per unit area of the excess column of denser liquid, p1 - p2 = (rho_m - rho) g dh
steps.why: The leads of the manometer are filled with the flowing liquid, so the U-tube measures the difference of p + rho g z between the two tappings. The pipe axis is horizontal, so this is the pressure difference p1 - p2 that enters Bernoulli's equation. In the manometer the column of U-tube liquid of height dh replaces an equal column of the flowing liquid, so the pressure difference is the difference in their weights per area. This gives the pressure drop without knowing either pressure.

steps.description: speed of the liquid in the wide section
steps.principle: Continuity equation A1 v1 = A2 v2 together with Bernoulli's equation for ideal flow at constant height, p1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = p2 + (1/2) rho v2^2, with the areas proportional to the squared diameters
steps.why: The liquid is incompressible and frictionless, so the same flow passes both sections and it speeds up in the throat to v2 = v1 (d1/d2)^2. The pressure drop is exactly what supplies the extra kinetic energy, dp = (1/2) rho v1^2 ((d1/d2)^4 - 1). Solving this for v1 turns the measured pressure drop into the speed in the wide section.

steps.description: volume flow rate through the pipe
steps.principle: Definition of the volume flow rate for a uniform speed: Q = A v, with the circular area A = pi d^2 / 4
steps.why: With a uniform speed across the section, the volume that passes the wide section per second is its area times the speed. By continuity the same flow passes the throat, so this is the flow rate through the pipe, which is what the question asks.

steps.text: Dimensional check: sqrt(Pa / (kg/m^3)) is a speed in m/s and area times speed is m^3/s. Limiting case: a zero reading means no flow, and for a given flow the reading grows as the throat is made narrower, so for a given reading a narrower throat means a smaller flow. Order of magnitude: about 1 m/s in a pipe of ten centimetres diameter is about ten litres per second, as obtained.

The Venturi meter converts a flow rate into a pressure difference between the wide section and the throat, and the U-tube measures that difference. steps.description: pressure difference between the wide section and the throat
steps.principle: Hydrostatic pressure law applied to the U-tube: the pressure difference between two tappings equals the weight per unit area of the excess column of denser liquid, p1 - p2 = (rho_m - rho) g dh
steps.why: The leads of the manometer are filled with the flowing liquid, so the U-tube measures the difference of p + rho g z between the two tappings. The pipe axis is horizontal, so this is the pressure difference p1 - p2 that enters Bernoulli's equation. In the manometer the column of U-tube liquid of height dh replaces an equal column of the flowing liquid, so the pressure difference is the difference in their weights per area. This gives the pressure drop without knowing either pressure.

steps.description: speed of the liquid in the wide section
steps.principle: Continuity equation A1 v1 = A2 v2 together with Bernoulli's equation for ideal flow at constant height, p1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = p2 + (1/2) rho v2^2, with the areas proportional to the squared diameters
steps.why: The liquid is incompressible and frictionless, so the same flow passes both sections and it speeds up in the throat to v2 = v1 (d1/d2)^2. The pressure drop is exactly what supplies the extra kinetic energy, dp = (1/2) rho v1^2 ((d1/d2)^4 - 1). Solving this for v1 turns the measured pressure drop into the speed in the wide section.

steps.description: volume flow rate through the pipe

steps.description: pressure difference between the wide section and the throat
steps.principle: Hydrostatic pressure law applied to the U-tube: the pressure difference between two tappings equals the weight per unit area of the excess column of denser liquid, p1 - p2 = (rho_m - rho) g dh
steps.why: The leads of the manometer are filled with the flowing liquid, so the U-tube measures the difference of p + rho g z between the two tappings. The pipe axis is horizontal, so this is the pressure difference p1 - p2 that enters Bernoulli's equation. In the manometer the column of U-tube liquid of height dh replaces an equal column of the flowing liquid, so the pressure difference is the difference in their weights per area. This gives the pressure drop without knowing either pressure.

steps.description: speed of the liquid in the wide section
steps.principle: Continuity equation A1 v1 = A2 v2 together with Bernoulli's equation for ideal flow at constant height, p1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = p2 + (1/2) rho v2^2, with the areas proportional to the squared diameters
steps.why: The liquid is incompressible and frictionless, so the same flow passes both sections and it speeds up in the throat to v2 = v1 (d1/d2)^2. The pressure drop is exactly what supplies the extra kinetic energy, dp = (1/2) rho v1^2 ((d1/d2)^4 - 1). Solving this for v1 turns the measured pressure drop into the speed in the wide section.

steps.description: volume flow rate through the pipe
steps.principle: Definition of the volume flow rate for a uniform speed: Q = A v, with the circular area A = pi d^2 / 4
steps.why: With a uniform speed across the section, the volume that passes the wide section per second is its area times the speed. By continuity the same flow passes the throat, so this is the flow rate through the pipe, which is what the question asks.

steps.text: The added sentence ("Before the flow was started, a further 5.1 m of tubing of the same bore was joined to the outlet end of the pipe, lengthening it.") gives q = 5.1 m. A further q of pipe of the same bore joined on gives the length L + q, so the pressure drop 128 eta (L + q) Q / (pi d^4) and the power dp Q grow with it. In the graph this changes the input L (length of the pipe): L' = L + q = 2 + 5.1 = 7.1 m. Every later step uses the changed L.

The pump power is the pressure drop along the pipe times the volume flow rate. The flow rate follows from the average speed and the area, and the pressure drop needed to drive that flow of a viscous liquid through the pipe follows from the Hagen-Poiseuille law; then multiply the two.

steps.description: volume flow rate
steps.principle: Definition of the volume flow rate in terms of the average speed, Q = A v, with the circular area A = pi d^2 / 4
steps.why: The Poiseuille law is written for the volume flow rate, but the problem gives the average speed over the cross-section, so the flow rate is the area of the cross-section times that average speed.

steps.description: pressure drop along the pipe
steps.principle: Hagen-Poiseuille law for steady laminar flow of a Newtonian liquid in a circular pipe, Q = pi R^4 dp / (8 eta L), that is dp = 8 eta L Q / (pi R^4) = 128 eta L Q / (pi d^4)
steps.why: In laminar flow the viscous shear stress balances the pressure force, which gives a parabolic velocity profile and a flow rate proportional to the pressure drop and to the fourth power of the radius. Inverting the law gives the pressure drop that drives the given flow rate through the stated length.

steps.description: power needed to drive the flow
steps.principle: Power as the rate of work done by the pressure force, P = dp Q
steps.why: The pump does work dp on every unit volume of liquid that it pushes through the pipe, so the power is the pressure drop times the volume per second. In steady flow this equals the rate at which viscous friction dissipates energy.

steps.text: Dimensional check: Pa s times m times m^3/s divided by m^4 is Pa, and Pa times m^3/s is W. Scaling: at a fixed flow rate the pressure drop goes as 1/d^4, so halving the diameter multiplies it by sixteen; at a fixed pipe the pressure drop is proportional to the speed, so doubling the speed makes the power four times larger.
power needed to drive the flow: 28.55 mW

Step 2. Given: d = 4 mm (inner diameter of the pipe; given); L = 2 m (length of the pipe; given); eta = 0.004 Pa*s (dynamic viscosity of the liquid; given); v = 20 cm/s (average speed of the liquid in the pipe; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The flow is steady, laminar and fully developed, the liquid is Newtonian and incompressible, and entrance effects are neglected. The pipe is straight and horizontal, so the pressure drop only drives the viscous flow.
Step 4. The added sentence ("Before the flow was started, a further 5.1 m of tubing of the same bore was joined to the outlet end of the pipe, lengthening it.") gives q = 5.1 m. A further q of pipe of the same bore joined on gives the length L + q, so the pressure drop 128 eta (L + q) Q / (pi d^4) and the power dp Q grow with it. In the graph this changes the input L (length of the pipe): L' = L + q = 2 + 5.1 = 7.1 m. Every later step uses the changed L.
Step 5. Approach: The pump power is the pressure drop along the pipe times the volume flow rate. The flow rate follows from the average speed and the area, and the pressure drop needed to drive that flow of a viscous liquid through the pipe follows from the Hagen-Poiseuille law; then multiply the two.
Step 6. Definition of the volume flow rate in terms of the average speed, Q = A v, with the circular area A = pi d^2 / 4. The Poiseuille law is written for the volume flow rate, but the problem gives the average speed over the cross-section, so the flow rate is the area of the cross-section times that average speed. Q = pi*d**2*v/4  (SI units). Q = pi*(0.004)**2*(0.2)/4 = 2.513e-06 (SI) = 2.513e-06 m³/s.
Step 7. Hagen-Poiseuille law for steady laminar flow of a Newtonian liquid in a circular pipe, Q = pi R^4 dp / (8 eta L), that is dp = 8 eta L Q / (pi R^4) = 128 eta L Q / (pi d^4). In laminar flow the viscous shear stress balances the pressure force, which gives a parabolic velocity profile and a flow rate proportional to the pressure drop and to the fourth power of the radius. Inverting the law gives the pressure drop that drives the given flow rate through the stated length. dp = 128*eta*L*Q/(pi*d**4)  (SI units). dp = 128*(0.004)*(7.1)*(2.513e-06)/(pi*(0.004)**4) = 1.136e+04 (SI) = 11.36 kPa.
Step 8. Power as the rate of work done by the pressure force, P = dp Q. The pump does work dp on every unit volume of liquid that it pushes through the pipe, so the power is the pressure drop times the volume per second. In steady flow this equals the rate at which viscous friction dissipates energy. P = dp*Q  (SI units). P = (1.136e+04)*(2.513e-06) = 0.02855 (SI) = 28.55 mW.
Step 9. Check: Dimensional check: Pa s times m times m^3/s divided by m^4 is Pa, and Pa times m^3/s is W. Scaling: at a fixed flow rate the pressure drop goes as 1/d^4, so halving the diameter multiplies it by sixteen; at a fixed pipe the pressure drop is proportional to the speed, so doubling the speed makes the power four times larger.
Step 10. Answer: power needed to drive the flow: 28.55 mW.

steps.text: No external force acts, so the momentum of the rocket and its exhaust is conserved. Applying this to the rocket as its mass falls gives the rocket equation; the final speed depends on the exhaust speed and on the ratio of the initial to the final mass.

Relation 2 that contains q: mass at the end of the burn m0 - r tb.
Relation 3 that contains q: dv = u r dt / m integrated over the burn time.

items.description: angular speed of the rotating hoop
items.name: Om

The bead rests in equilibrium relative to the hoop at a point away from the axis, the stable point that exists because the hoop turns faster than the critical rate, and the oscillations are small and along the hoop.

steps.text: Work in the frame of the hoop, where the bead feels gravity and the centrifugal force. Find the equilibrium angle from the condition that the effective potential is stationary, then expand the Lagrangian to second order in the displacement.

steps.description: cosine of the polar angle of the equilibrium position, measured from the downward vertical

steps.description: sine of the polar angle of the equilibrium position
steps.principle: Trigonometric identity: sin theta_0 = sqrt(1 - cos^2 theta_0)
steps.why: The curvature of the effective potential is needed at the equilibrium angle and involves its sine.

steps.description: angular frequency of small oscillations about the equilibrium
steps.principle: Small oscillations: theta'' = -Om^2 sin^2 theta_0 (theta - theta_0), so the angular frequency is Om sin theta_0
steps.why: Expanding the equation of motion to first order about the equilibrium gives a harmonic equation whose stiffness per unit inertia is Om^2 sin^2 theta_0; the mass of the bead has divided out.

steps.description: period of small oscillations about the equilibrium
steps.principle: Period of a harmonic oscillation, T = 2 pi / omega
steps.why: The small oscillations are harmonic, so the period is two pi over their angular frequency.

steps.text: As the rotation rate grows, sin theta_0 tends to one and the period tends to 2 pi / Om; near the critical rate the period grows without limit, because the restoring force vanishes.

The skaters hold on to each other and move off together after the collision, a perfectly inelastic collision, and their velocities before it are perpendicular.

steps.text: The momentum of the system is conserved in the collision; the two perpendicular components give the velocity after it. The kinetic energy converted is the energy before minus the energy after.

steps.description: kinetic energy before the collision
steps.principle: Kinetic energy of the system before the collision, the sum of (1/2) m v^2 for each skater
steps.why: Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the two skaters' energies add whatever their directions.

steps.description: total mass of the two skaters
steps.principle: Total mass of a system that moves as one body after the collision, M = m1 + m2
steps.why: The skaters hold on to each other, so the final momentum is carried by the combined mass.

steps.description: eastward momentum of the system
steps.principle: Momentum of the eastward skater, p = m1 v1
steps.why: Only this skater moves east, so it carries all the eastward momentum.

steps.description: northward momentum of the system
steps.principle: Momentum of the northward skater, p = m2 v2
steps.why: Only this skater moves north, so it carries all the northward momentum.

steps.description: speed of the two skaters together after the collision
steps.principle: Conservation of momentum for each perpendicular component: the final speed is the magnitude of the vector sum divided by M
steps.why: The two components are perpendicular, so the magnitude of the total momentum is the root of the sum of squares; dividing by the total mass gives the final speed.

steps.description: kinetic energy after the collision
steps.principle: Kinetic energy of the combined body after the collision, (1/2) M Vf^2
steps.why: After the collision the two skaters move together at the final speed.

steps.description: kinetic energy converted to other forms in the collision
steps.principle: Energy accounting: the kinetic energy converted to other forms is the initial minus the final kinetic energy
steps.why: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not in a perfectly inelastic collision; the difference goes into deformation and heat.

steps.text: The result equals one half of the reduced mass times the square of the relative speed, which is independent of the frame of the observer; it is positive, as it must be for an inelastic collision.

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the kinetic energy converted to other forms in the collision, in J.
Step 2. Given: m1 = 60 kg (mass of the skater moving east; given); v1 = 4 m/s (speed of the skater moving east; given); m2 = 75 kg (mass of the skater moving north; given); v2 = 3 m/s (speed of the skater moving north; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The ice is frictionless and level, and the collision is brief, so only the two skaters exchange momentum. The skaters hold on to each other and move off together after the collision, a perfectly inelastic collision, and their velocities before it are perpendicular.
Step 4. Approach: The momentum of the system is conserved in the collision; the two perpendicular components give the velocity after it. The kinetic energy converted is the energy before minus the energy after.
Step 5. Kinetic energy of the system before the collision, the sum of (1/2) m v^2 for each skater. Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the two skaters' energies add whatever their directions. Ki = (m1*v1**2 + m2*v2**2)/2  (SI units). Ki = ((60)*(4)**2 + (75)*(3)**2)/2 = 817.5 (SI) = 817.5 J.
Step 6. Total mass of a system that moves as one body after the collision, M = m1 + m2. The skaters hold on to each other, so the final momentum is carried by the combined mass. M = m1 + m2  (SI units). M = (60) + (75) = 135 (SI) = 135 kg.
Step 7. Momentum of the eastward skater, p = m1 v1. Only this skater moves east, so it carries all the eastward momentum. px = m1*v1  (SI units). px = (60)*(4) = 240 (SI) = 240 kg*m/s.
Step 8. Momentum of the northward skater, p = m2 v2. Only this skater moves north, so it carries all the northward momentum. py = m2*v2  (SI units). py = (75)*(3) = 225 (SI) = 225 kg*m/s.
Step 9. Conservation of momentum for each perpendicular component: the final speed is the magnitude of the vector sum divided by M. The two components are perpendicular, so the magnitude of the total momentum is the root of the sum of squares; dividing by the total mass gives the final speed. Vf = sqrt(px**2 + py**2)/M  (SI units). Vf = sqrt((240)**2 + (225)**2)/(135) = 2.437 (SI) = 2.437 m/s.
Step 10. Kinetic energy of the combined body after the collision, (1/2) M Vf^2. After the collision the two skaters move together at the final speed. Kf = M*Vf**2/2  (SI units). Kf = (135)*(2.437)**2/2 = 400.8 (SI) = 400.8 J.
Step 11. Energy accounting: the kinetic energy converted to other forms is the initial minus the final kinetic energy. Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not in a perfectly inelastic collision; the difference goes into deformation and heat. dK = Ki - Kf  (SI units). dK = (817.5) - (400.8) = 416.7 (SI) = 416.7 J.
Step 12. Check: The result equals one half of the reduced mass times the square of the relative speed, which is independent of the frame of the observer; it is positive, as it must be for an inelastic collision.
Step 13. Answer: kinetic energy converted to other forms in the collision: 416.7 J.

steps.description: kinetic energy before the collision
steps.principle: Kinetic energy of the system before the collision, the sum of (1/2) m v^2 for each skater
steps.why: Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the two skaters' energies add whatever their directions.

steps.description: total mass of the two skaters
steps.principle: Total mass of a system that moves as one body after the collision, M = m1 + m2
steps.why: The skaters hold on to each other, so the final momentum is carried by the combined mass.

steps.description: eastward momentum of the system
steps.principle: Momentum of the eastward skater, p = m1 v1
steps.why: Only this skater moves east, so it carries all the eastward momentum.

steps.description: northward momentum of the system
steps.principle: Momentum of the northward skater, p = m2 v2
steps.why: Only this skater moves north, so it carries all the northward momentum.

steps.description: speed of the two skaters together after the collision
steps.principle: Conservation of momentum for each perpendicular component: the final speed is the magnitude of the vector sum divided by M
steps.why: The two components are perpendicular, so the magnitude of the total momentum is the root of the sum of squares; dividing by the total mass gives the final speed.

steps.description: kinetic energy after the collision
steps.principle: Kinetic energy of the combined body after the collision, (1/2) M Vf^2
steps.why: After the collision the two skaters move together at the final speed.

steps.description: kinetic energy converted to other forms in the collision
steps.principle: Energy accounting: the kinetic energy converted to other forms is the initial minus the final kinetic energy
steps.why: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not in a perfectly inelastic collision; the difference goes into deformation and heat.

steps.text: The result equals one half of the reduced mass times the square of the relative speed, which is independent of the frame of the observer; it is positive, as it must be for an inelastic collision.

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the kinetic energy converted to other forms in the collision, in J.
Step 2. Given: m1 = 60 kg (mass of the skater moving east; given); v1 = 4 m/s (speed of the skater moving east; given); m2 = 75 kg (mass of the skater moving north; given); v2 = 3 m/s (speed of the skater moving north; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The ice is frictionless and level, and the collision is brief, so only the two skaters exchange momentum. The skaters hold on to each other and move off together after the collision, a perfectly inelastic collision, and their velocities before it are perpendicular.
Step 4. The added sentence ("A 12 kg bag is carried by the coach.") gives 12 kg. This quantity has no path to the target: a bag carried by the coach adds to the coach's load only; the two colliding skaters keep their stated masses. It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.
Step 5. Approach: The momentum of the system is conserved in the collision; the two perpendicular components give the velocity after it. The kinetic energy converted is the energy before minus the energy after.
Step 6. Kinetic energy of the system before the collision, the sum of (1/2) m v^2 for each skater. Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the two skaters' energies add whatever their directions. Ki = (m1*v1**2 + m2*v2**2)/2  (SI units). Ki = ((60)*(4)**2 + (75)*(3)**2)/2 = 817.5 (SI) = 817.5 J.
Step 7. Total mass of a system that moves as one body after the collision, M = m1 + m2. The skaters hold on to each other, so the final momentum is carried by the combined mass. M = m1 + m2  (SI units). M = (60) + (75) = 135 (SI) = 135 kg.
Step 8. Momentum of the eastward skater, p = m1 v1. Only this skater moves east, so it carries all the eastward momentum. px = m1*v1  (SI units). px = (60)*(4) = 240 (SI) = 240 kg*m/s.
Step 9. Momentum of the northward skater, p = m2 v2. Only this skater moves north, so it carries all the northward momentum. py = m2*v2  (SI units). py = (75)*(3) = 225 (SI) = 225 kg*m/s.
Step 10. Conservation of momentum for each perpendicular component: the final speed is the magnitude of the vector sum divided by M. The two components are perpendicular, so the magnitude of the total momentum is the root of the sum of squares; dividing by the total mass gives the final speed. Vf = sqrt(px**2 + py**2)/M  (SI units). Vf = sqrt((240)**2 + (225)**2)/(135) = 2.437 (SI) = 2.437 m/s.
Step 11. Kinetic energy of the combined body after the collision, (1/2) M Vf^2. After the collision the two skaters move together at the final speed. Kf = M*Vf**2/2  (SI units). Kf = (135)*(2.437)**2/2 = 400.8 (SI) = 400.8 J.
Step 12. Energy accounting: the kinetic energy converted to other forms is the initial minus the final kinetic energy. Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not in a perfectly inelastic collision; the difference goes into deformation and heat. dK = Ki - Kf  (SI units). dK = (817.5) - (400.8) = 416.7 (SI) = 416.7 J.
Step 13. Check: The result equals one half of the reduced mass times the square of the relative speed, which is independent of the frame of the observer; it is positive, as it must be for an inelastic collision.

items: The turntable is horizontal and rigid and turns about its vertical axis with a constant angular acceleration from rest.

The coin does not slip: it stays at the same place on the turntable, so its acceleration is that of the point of the turntable under it, and the friction force is the force that gives it this acceleration.

steps.text: The coin has not slipped, so its acceleration equals that of the point of the turntable under it. That acceleration has a centripetal part from the angular speed at the given time and a tangential part from the angular acceleration; the friction force is the mass times the vector sum.

steps.principle: Rotational kinematics with constant angular acceleration from rest: w = alpha t
steps.why: The angular speed at the given time fixes the centripetal acceleration of the coin.

steps.principle: Centripetal acceleration of circular motion, a_c = w^2 r
steps.why: The coin moves on a circle of radius r at the angular speed found, so it needs this acceleration toward the axis.

steps.description: magnitude of the friction force of the turntable on the coin
steps.principle: Newton's second law for the coin: the friction force is m times the vector sum of the two perpendicular accelerations
steps.why: The only horizontal force on the coin is static friction, so it must supply both accelerations; the two are perpendicular and combine as the root of the sum of squares.

Step 2. Given: m = 12 g (mass of the coin; given); r = 8 cm (distance of the coin from the axis of the turntable; given); alpha = 0.9 rad/s² (constant angular acceleration of the turntable; given); t = 4 s (time since the turntable started from rest; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The turntable is horizontal and rigid and turns about its vertical axis with a constant angular acceleration from rest. The coin does not slip: it stays at the same place on the turntable, so its acceleration is that of the point of the turntable under it, and the friction force is the force that gives it this acceleration.
Step 4. Approach: The coin has not slipped, so its acceleration equals that of the point of the turntable under it. That acceleration has a centripetal part from the angular speed at the given time and a tangential part from the angular acceleration; the friction force is the mass times the vector sum.
Step 5. Tangential acceleration of a point at radius r with angular acceleration alpha, a_t = alpha r. The turntable is speeding up, so the coin also needs an acceleration along its path. at = alpha*r  (SI units). at = (0.9)*(0.08) = 0.072 (SI) = 0.072 m/s².
Step 6. Rotational kinematics with constant angular acceleration from rest: w = alpha t. The angular speed at the given time fixes the centripetal acceleration of the coin. w = alpha*t  (SI units). w = (0.9)*(4) = 3.6 (SI) = 3.6 rad/s.
Step 7. Centripetal acceleration of circular motion, a_c = w^2 r. The coin moves on a circle of radius r at the angular speed found, so it needs this acceleration toward the axis. ac = w**2*r  (SI units). ac = (3.6)**2*(0.08) = 1.037 (SI) = 1.037 m/s².
Step 8. Newton's second law for the coin: the friction force is m times the vector sum of the two perpendicular accelerations. The only horizontal force on the coin is static friction, so it must supply both accelerations; the two are perpendicular and combine as the root of the sum of squares. f = m*sqrt(ac**2 + at**2)  (SI units). f = (0.012)*sqrt((1.037)**2 + (0.072)**2) = 0.01247 (SI) = 12.47 mN.

Step 10. Answer: friction force of the turntable on the coin: 12.47 mN.

items.name: r

items.description: constant angular acceleration of the turntable
items.name: alpha

items.description: time since the turntable started from rest

items: The turntable is horizontal and rigid and turns about its vertical axis with a constant angular acceleration from rest.

The coin does not slip: it stays at the same place on the turntable, so its acceleration is that of the point of the turntable under it, and the friction force is the force that gives it this acceleration.

steps.text: The added sentence ("A 7 g washer was taped to the coin before the turntable was started.") gives q = 7 g. A washer taped to the coin travels with it, so the mass that has to be accelerated becomes m + q and the friction force grows with it. In the graph this changes the input m (mass of the coin): m' = m + q = 12 + 7 = 19 g. Every later step uses the changed m.

The coin has not slipped, so its acceleration equals that of the point of the turntable under it. That acceleration has a centripetal part from the angular speed at the given time and a tangential part from the angular acceleration; the friction force is the mass times the vector sum.

steps.description: tangential acceleration of the coin
steps.principle: Tangential acceleration of a point at radius r with angular acceleration alpha, a_t = alpha r
steps.why: The turntable is speeding up, so the coin also needs an acceleration along its path.

steps.description: angular speed of the turntable
steps.principle: Rotational kinematics with constant angular acceleration from rest: w = alpha t
steps.why: The angular speed at the given time fixes the centripetal acceleration of the coin.

steps.description: centripetal acceleration of the coin
steps.principle: Centripetal acceleration of circular motion, a_c = w^2 r
steps.why: The coin moves on a circle of radius r at the angular speed found, so it needs this acceleration toward the axis.

steps.description: magnitude of the friction force of the turntable on the coin
steps.principle: Newton's second law for the coin: the friction force is m times the vector sum of the two perpendicular accelerations
steps.why: The only horizontal force on the coin is static friction, so it must supply both accelerations; the two are perpendicular and combine as the root of the sum of squares.

steps.text: With no angular acceleration the result reduces to m w^2 r; units: kg times m/s^2 give N, shown in millinewtons.
friction force of the turntable on the coin: 19.75 mN

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the friction force of the turntable on the coin, in mN.
Step 2. Given: m = 12 g (mass of the coin; given); r = 8 cm (distance of the coin from the axis of the turntable; given); alpha = 0.9 rad/s² (constant angular acceleration of the turntable; given); t = 4 s (time since the turntable started from rest; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The turntable is horizontal and rigid and turns about its vertical axis with a constant angular acceleration from rest. The coin does not slip: it stays at the same place on the turntable, so its acceleration is that of the point of the turntable under it, and the friction force is the force that gives it this acceleration.
Step 4. The added sentence ("A 7 g washer was taped to the coin before the turntable was started.") gives q = 7 g. A washer taped to the coin travels with it, so the mass that has to be accelerated becomes m + q and the friction force grows with it. In the graph this changes the input m (mass of the coin): m' = m + q = 12 + 7 = 19 g. Every later step uses the changed m.
Step 5. Approach: The coin has not slipped, so its acceleration equals that of the point of the turntable under it. That acceleration has a centripetal part from the angular speed at the given time and a tangential part from the angular acceleration; the friction force is the mass times the vector sum.
Step 6. Tangential acceleration of a point at radius r with angular acceleration alpha, a_t = alpha r. The turntable is speeding up, so the coin also needs an acceleration along its path. at = alpha*r  (SI units). at = (0.9)*(0.08) = 0.072 (SI) = 0.072 m/s².
Step 7. Rotational kinematics with constant angular acceleration from rest: w = alpha t. The angular speed at the given time fixes the centripetal acceleration of the coin. w = alpha*t  (SI units). w = (0.9)*(4) = 3.6 (SI) = 3.6 rad/s.
Step 8. Centripetal acceleration of circular motion, a_c = w^2 r. The coin moves on a circle of radius r at the angular speed found, so it needs this acceleration toward the axis. ac = w**2*r  (SI units). ac = (3.6)**2*(0.08) = 1.037 (SI) = 1.037 m/s².
Step 9. Newton's second law for the coin: the friction force is m times the vector sum of the two perpendicular accelerations. The only horizontal force on the coin is static friction, so it must supply both accelerations; the two are perpendicular and combine as the root of the sum of squares. f = m*sqrt(ac**2 + at**2)  (SI units). f = (0.019)*sqrt((1.037)**2 + (0.072)**2) = 0.01975 (SI) = 19.75 mN.
Step 10. Check: With no angular acceleration the result reduces to m w^2 r; units: kg times m/s^2 give N, shown in millinewtons.
Step 11. Answer: friction force of the turntable on the coin: 19.75 mN.

items.description: depth of the liquid in the tank at rest
items.name: h0

items: g is a uniform constant of the stated value.

The liquid has reached a steady state in which it turns with the tank as a solid body at the stated angular speed; the tank is a vertical cylinder turning about its axis and open at the top, and it is tall enough that no liquid spills.
The pressure at the free surface is atmospheric, and surface tension and the viscosity of the liquid do not matter in the steady state.

steps.text: In the frame of the rotating tank the liquid is at rest under gravity and the centrifugal force, so its free surface is a paraboloid. The volume of the liquid is conserved, which fixes the height of the surface at the axis.

steps.description: height of the liquid surface at the wall above its height at the axis
steps.principle: Free surface of a rotating liquid (hydrostatic balance in the rotating frame): z(r) = z0 + w^2 r^2 / (2 g), so the rise from axis to wall is w^2 R^2 / (2 g)
steps.why: The pressure is constant on the surface, which is perpendicular to the effective gravity; integrating the slope w^2 r / g gives the paraboloid and its total rise.

steps.description: depth of the liquid at the wall of the tank
steps.principle: Conservation of the volume of liquid: the mean depth stays h0, and the mean height of a paraboloid above its vertex is half of the rise, so the depth at the wall is h0 + dh / 2
steps.why: The average of w^2 r^2 / (2 g) weighted by the area is half of its value at the wall, so the surface at the wall is half of the rise above the original level.

steps.description: depth of the liquid at the axis of the tank
steps.principle: Depth at the axis from the depth at the wall minus the rise: ha = hw - dh
steps.why: The surface is lowest at the axis, below the wall level by the full rise of the paraboloid.

steps.text: With no rotation the result is h0; the liquid is lowered at the axis by half of the rise and raised at the wall by half of it, and the density of the liquid does not appear.

items: The two discs are coaxial on a frictionless axle, so no external torque acts on the pair about the axle.
The faces grip each other and slip against each other until the two discs turn together at one angular speed; the energy that is not kept as rotational kinetic energy is dissipated as heat.

steps.text: No external torque acts on the two discs about the common axle, so their total angular momentum is conserved while they slip and then turn together. The kinetic energy that is lost is the difference between the energy before and after.

steps.description: moment of inertia of the spinning disc about the axle
steps.principle: Moment of inertia of a uniform solid disc about its axis, I = (1/2) m r^2
steps.why: The spinning disc is a uniform solid disc, so its moment of inertia about the axle through its centre follows from its mass and radius; this is the number that enters angular momentum and energy.

steps.description: rotational kinetic energy before the coupling
steps.principle: Rotational kinetic energy of a rigid body, K = (1/2) I w^2, for the spinning disc alone
steps.why: Before the contact only the first disc turns, so the energy of the system is the energy of that disc.

steps.description: common angular speed of the two discs after the coupling
steps.principle: Conservation of angular momentum about the axle: I1 w1 = (I1 + I2) wf
steps.why: The faces exert equal and opposite torques on each other and nothing else exerts a torque, so the sum of the angular momenta is unchanged; solving for the common speed gives wf.

steps.description: rotational kinetic energy after the coupling
steps.principle: Rotational kinetic energy of the two discs turning together, K = (1/2) (I1 + I2) wf^2
steps.why: After the coupling the two discs are one rotating body with the combined moment of inertia.

steps.description: mechanical energy dissipated as heat in the coupling
steps.principle: Energy accounting: the mechanical energy that is not kept as rotational kinetic energy is dissipated as heat, dE = Ki - Kf
steps.why: Angular momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not while the faces slip, so the difference is the heat generated.

steps.text: The result equals one half of the reduced moment of inertia I1 I2 / (I1 + I2) times the square of the initial angular speed; it is positive and does not depend on the friction torque of the faces.

steps.text: Find the initial acceleration of the bead, in m/s².

items.description: field magnitude at the surface of the ball before the cavity was cut
items.name: E0

items.description: distance from the centre of the ball to the centre of the cavity
items.name: d

items: The ball is an insulator whose remaining charge stays fixed where it was, spread uniformly through the solid material; the bead is small enough not to disturb that charge.
The cavity is spherical, empty and wholly inside the ball.
Gravity is neglected and the bead is released from rest.

steps.text: Treat the ball with the cavity as a whole ball of uniform charge density plus a ball of opposite charge density that fills the cavity. Inside a uniformly charged ball the field grows in proportion to the distance from its centre, so the two fields subtract to a uniform field in the cavity, which gives the force and then the acceleration.

steps.description: field in the cavity
steps.principle: Superposition with Gauss's law for a uniformly charged ball: inside the ball the field is E(r) = E_surface r/R, directed away from the centre, so the whole ball gives E0 r1/R and the cavity ball of opposite charge gives -E0 r2/R
steps.why: At a point of the cavity the two position vectors differ by the vector from the ball's centre to the cavity's centre, so the fields add to E0 d/R, the same everywhere in the cavity and pointing along the line of centres.

steps.description: electric force on the bead
steps.principle: Electric force on a charge: F = q E for a charge in an electric field
steps.why: The field in the cavity is uniform and the bead is small, so the force on it is its charge times that field.

steps.description: initial acceleration of the bead
steps.principle: Newton's second law: acceleration = force / mass, with gravity neglected
steps.why: The electric force is the only force on the bead, so dividing it by the mass gives the initial acceleration.

steps.text: If the cavity were centred on the ball (d = 0) the field in it must vanish, and the formula gives zero; the field must grow in proportion to d, and the point of release inside the cavity cannot matter because the field is uniform.
initial acceleration of the bead: 48 m/s²

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the initial acceleration of the bead, in m/s².
Step 2. Given: E0 = 40 kV/m (field magnitude at the surface of the ball before the cavity was cut; given); R = 20 cm (radius of the ball; given); d = 6 cm (distance from the centre of the ball to the centre of the cavity; given); q0 = 2 μC (charge of the bead; given); m = 0.5 g (mass of the bead; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The ball is an insulator whose remaining charge stays fixed where it was, spread uniformly through the solid material; the bead is small enough not to disturb that charge. The cavity is spherical, empty and wholly inside the ball. Gravity is neglected and the bead is released from rest.
Step 4. Approach: Treat the ball with the cavity as a whole ball of uniform charge density plus a ball of opposite charge density that fills the cavity. Inside a uniformly charged ball the field grows in proportion to the distance from its centre, so the two fields subtract to a uniform field in the cavity, which gives the force and then the acceleration.
Step 5. Superposition with Gauss's law for a uniformly charged ball: inside the ball the field is E(r) = E_surface r/R, directed away from the centre, so the whole ball gives E0 r1/R and the cavity ball of opposite charge gives -E0 r2/R. At a point of the cavity the two position vectors differ by the vector from the ball's centre to the cavity's centre, so the fields add to E0 d/R, the same everywhere in the cavity and pointing along the line of centres. Ecav = E0*d/R  (SI units). Ecav = (4e+04)*(0.06)/(0.2) = 1.2e+04 (SI) = 12 kV/m.
Step 6. Electric force on a charge: F = q E for a charge in an electric field. The field in the cavity is uniform and the bead is small, so the force on it is its charge times that field. F = q0*Ecav  (SI units). F = (2e-06)*(1.2e+04) = 0.024 (SI) = 24 mN.
Step 7. Newton's second law: acceleration = force / mass, with gravity neglected. The electric force is the only force on the bead, so dividing it by the mass gives the initial acceleration. a = F/m  (SI units). a = (0.024)/(0.0005) = 48 (SI) = 48 m/s².
Step 8. Check: If the cavity were centred on the ball (d = 0) the field in it must vanish, and the formula gives zero; the field must grow in proportion to d, and the point of release inside the cavity cannot matter because the field is uniform.
Step 9. Answer: initial acceleration of the bead: 48 m/s².

Step 3. Assumptions: The ball is an insulator whose remaining charge stays fixed where it was, spread uniformly through the solid material; the bead is small enough not to disturb that charge. The cavity is spherical, empty and wholly inside the ball. Gravity is neglected and the bead is released from rest.
Step 4. The added sentence ("An uncharged 0.7 g plastic clip is attached to the bead before it is released.") gives q = 0.7 g. An uncharged clip attached to the bead adds its mass to the mass of the bead, so m becomes m + q while the charge of the bead is unchanged. In the graph this changes the input m (mass of the bead): m' = m + q = 0.5 + 0.7 = 1.2 g. Every later step uses the changed m.
Step 5. Approach: Treat the ball with the cavity as a whole ball of uniform charge density plus a ball of opposite charge density that fills the cavity. Inside a uniformly charged ball the field grows in proportion to the distance from its centre, so the two fields subtract to a uniform field in the cavity, which gives the force and then the acceleration.
Step 6. Superposition with Gauss's law for a uniformly charged ball: inside the ball the field is E(r) = E_surface r/R, directed away from the centre, so the whole ball gives E0 r1/R and the cavity ball of opposite charge gives -E0 r2/R. At a point of the cavity the two position vectors differ by the vector from the ball's centre to the cavity's centre, so the fields add to E0 d/R, the same everywhere in the cavity and pointing along the line of centres. Ecav = E0*d/R  (SI units). Ecav = (4e+04)*(0.06)/(0.2) = 1.2e+04 (SI) = 12 kV/m.

Step 10. Answer: initial acceleration of the bead: 20 m/s².

steps.text: Find the capacitance that puts the supply current in phase with the voltage, in μF.

items: The motor is a resistor in series with an inductor of the stated values, and its impedance does not depend on the capacitor.
The supply is an ideal sinusoidal voltage source of the stated frequency and the capacitor is ideal.

steps.text: The supply current is in phase with the voltage when the total admittance is purely real. The motor branch has an inductive part to its admittance, and the capacitor must supply an equal and opposite susceptance.

steps.description: reactance of the winding
steps.principle: Inductive reactance: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L
steps.why: The coil's reactance at the supply frequency sets the quadrature part of the motor's impedance.

steps.description: magnitude of the impedance of the motor
steps.principle: Magnitude of a series R-L impedance: |Z| = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2)
steps.why: The resistance and reactance are in quadrature, so the impedance magnitude is their root sum of squares, which gives the admittance Y = 1/(R + j X_L) = (R - j X_L)/|Z|^2.

steps.description: capacitance that cancels the quadrature current
steps.principle: Condition for unity power factor: the capacitor's susceptance omega C equals the motor's inductive susceptance X_L/|Z|^2, so C = X_L/(omega |Z|^2)
steps.why: The motor branch contributes -j X_L/|Z|^2 to the admittance and the capacitor contributes +j omega C; the imaginary parts cancel when they are equal, whatever the supply voltage is.

steps.text: With R = 0 the formula reduces to C = 1/(omega^2 L), the capacitor that resonates with the coil in parallel; a larger resistance needs a smaller capacitance, and the result must be positive.
capacitance that puts the supply current in phase with the voltage: 144.2 μF

Step 3. Assumptions: The motor is a resistor in series with an inductor of the stated values, and its impedance does not depend on the capacitor. The supply is an ideal sinusoidal voltage source of the stated frequency and the capacitor is ideal.
Step 4. Approach: The supply current is in phase with the voltage when the total admittance is purely real. The motor branch has an inductive part to its admittance, and the capacitor must supply an equal and opposite susceptance.
Step 5. Inductive reactance: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L. The coil's reactance at the supply frequency sets the quadrature part of the motor's impedance. XL = 2*pi*f*L  (SI units). XL = 2*pi*(50)*(0.05) = 15.71 (SI) = 15.71 Ω.
Step 6. Magnitude of a series R-L impedance: |Z| = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2). The resistance and reactance are in quadrature, so the impedance magnitude is their root sum of squares, which gives the admittance Y = 1/(R + j X_L) = (R - j X_L)/|Z|^2. Zmag = sqrt(R**2 + XL**2)  (SI units). Zmag = sqrt((10)**2 + (15.71)**2) = 18.62 (SI) = 18.62 Ω.
Step 7. Condition for unity power factor: the capacitor's susceptance omega C equals the motor's inductive susceptance X_L/|Z|^2, so C = X_L/(omega |Z|^2). The motor branch contributes -j X_L/|Z|^2 to the admittance and the capacitor contributes +j omega C; the imaginary parts cancel when they are equal, whatever the supply voltage is. C = XL/(2*pi*f*Zmag**2)  (SI units). C = (15.71)/(2*pi*(50)*(18.62)**2) = 0.0001442 (SI) = 144.2 μF.
Step 8. Check: With R = 0 the formula reduces to C = 1/(omega^2 L), the capacitor that resonates with the coil in parallel; a larger resistance needs a smaller capacitance, and the result must be positive.

steps.text: Find the displacement of the spot on the screen, in cm.

items.description: potential difference across the deflecting plates
items.name: Vd

items.description: distance from the ends of the plates to the screen
items.name: L

items: The ions all have the same charge and mass, start from rest, and move non-relativistically in a vacuum.
The field between the plates is uniform and perpendicular to the beam, and zero outside the plates; the ions enter midway between the plates, parallel to them, and leave without striking them.
Beyond the plates the ions move in a straight line to the screen; gravity is neglected.

steps.text: The ions gain their speed from the accelerating voltage. Between the plates they feel a constant sideways force and acquire a sideways velocity and displacement; beyond the plates they drift in a straight line. The ratio of the sideways to the forward velocity depends only on the two voltages and the geometry.

steps.description: tangent of the deflection angle on leaving the plates
steps.principle: Kinematics of a charge in crossed motion: the forward speed v satisfies (1/2) m v^2 = q Va, the sideways acceleration is q Vd/(m d) for a time ell/v, so tan(theta) = v_y/v = Vd ell/(2 d Va)
steps.why: The charge and mass of the ions cancel in the ratio of the sideways velocity to the forward velocity, so the deflection angle follows from the voltages and the plate geometry.

steps.description: sideways displacement on leaving the plates
steps.principle: Uniform sideways acceleration over the plate length: the displacement is half the final sideways velocity times the transit time, so y_exit = tan(theta) ell/2
steps.why: The sideways displacement grows quadratically with time, so at the plate exit it is half of tan(theta) times the plate length.

steps.description: displacement of the spot from the undeflected position
steps.principle: Straight-line motion beyond the plates: the spot is displaced by y_exit + L tan(theta)
steps.why: After the plates no force acts, so the ions keep the exit direction and add L tan(theta) over the drift distance.

steps.text: The same result follows by extrapolating the exit ray backwards to the midpoint of the plates, giving tan(theta)(L + ell/2); doubling the plate voltage doubles the displacement and doubling the accelerating voltage halves it.
displacement of the spot on the screen: 4.062 cm

Step 2. Given: Va = 2000 V (accelerating potential difference; given); Vd = 100 V (potential difference across the deflecting plates; given); ell = 5 cm (length of the deflecting plates; given); d = 1 cm (separation of the deflecting plates; given); L = 30 cm (distance from the ends of the plates to the screen; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The ions all have the same charge and mass, start from rest, and move non-relativistically in a vacuum. The field between the plates is uniform and perpendicular to the beam, and zero outside the plates; the ions enter midway between the plates, parallel to them, and leave without striking them. The ratio of the sideways to the forward velocity depends only on the two voltages and the geometry.

The charge and mass of the ions cancel in the ratio of the sideways velocity to the forward velocity, so the deflection angle follows from the voltages and the plate geometry. tanth = Vd*ell/(2*d*Va)  (SI units). tanth = (100)*(0.05)/(2*(0.01)*(2000)) = 0.125 (SI) = 0.125.

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the total charge that flows round the coil, in mC.
Step 2. Given: B0 = 80 mT (initial field strength inside the solenoid; given); rc = 3 cm (radius of the coil; given); N = 200 (number of turns of the coil; given); R = 12 Ω (resistance of the coil circuit; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The field inside the solenoid is uniform and parallel to the axis, and zero outside it; the coil is coaxial with the solenoid and lies entirely inside it. The self-inductance of the coil is negligible and its resistance is constant.
Step 4. Approach: The change of flux through the coil, times the number of turns, divided by the resistance, is the charge that flows; the time over which the field falls does not matter. Find the flux through one turn, then the charge.
Step 5. Area of a circular turn: A = pi r^2. The coil lies entirely inside the uniform field, so the flux is the field times the area enclosed by one turn. A = pi*rc**2  (SI units). A = pi*(0.03)**2 = 0.002827 (SI) = 28.27 cm².
Step 6. Magnetic flux through a loop perpendicular to a uniform field: Phi = B A, so the change of flux is B0 A. The field falls from B0 to zero, so the flux through each turn falls by B0 A. Phi = B0*A  (SI units). Phi = (0.08)*(0.002827) = 0.0002262 (SI) = 0.2262 mWb.
Step 7. Faraday's law and Ohm's law: emf = N dPhi/dt and I = emf/R, so the charge Q = integral of I dt = N Delta Phi / R. The induced emf is the rate of change of the flux linkage; integrating the current over the time of the change leaves the total change of flux linkage divided by the resistance. Q = N*Phi/R  (SI units). Q = (200)*(0.0002262)/(12) = 0.00377 (SI) = 3.77 mC.
Step 8. Check: The result does not contain the time taken, as it must for a total charge; doubling the number of turns doubles the flux linkage but not the resistance, so it doubles the charge.
Step 9. Answer: total charge that flows round the coil: 3.77 mC.

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the total charge that flows round the coil, in mC.
Step 2. Given: B0 = 80 mT (initial field strength inside the solenoid; given); rc = 3 cm (radius of the coil; given); N = 200 (number of turns of the coil; given); R = 12 Ω (resistance of the coil circuit; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The field inside the solenoid is uniform and parallel to the axis, and zero outside it; the coil is coaxial with the solenoid and lies entirely inside it. The self-inductance of the coil is negligible and its resistance is constant.
Step 4. Approach: The change of flux through the coil, times the number of turns, divided by the resistance, is the charge that flows; the time over which the field falls does not matter. Find the flux through one turn, then the charge.
Step 5. Area of a circular turn: A = pi r^2. The coil lies entirely inside the uniform field, so the flux is the field times the area enclosed by one turn. A = pi*rc**2  (SI units). A = pi*(0.03)**2 = 0.002827 (SI) = 28.27 cm².
Step 6. Magnetic flux through a loop perpendicular to a uniform field: Phi = B A, so the change of flux is B0 A. The field falls from B0 to zero, so the flux through each turn falls by B0 A. Phi = B0*A  (SI units). Phi = (0.08)*(0.002827) = 0.0002262 (SI) = 0.2262 mWb.
Step 7. Faraday's law and Ohm's law: emf = N dPhi/dt and I = emf/R, so the charge Q = integral of I dt = N Delta Phi / R. The induced emf is the rate of change of the flux linkage; integrating the current over the time of the change leaves the total change of flux linkage divided by the resistance. Q = N*Phi/R  (SI units). Q = (200)*(0.0002262)/(12) = 0.00377 (SI) = 3.77 mC.
Step 8. Check: The result does not contain the time taken, as it must for a total charge; doubling the number of turns doubles the flux linkage but not the resistance, so it doubles the charge.
Step 9. Answer: total charge that flows round the coil: 3.77 mC.

items: The cable is lossless, with inductance and capacitance spread uniformly along it; its length does not enter the answer.

steps.text: A step on a lossless line launches a wave whose voltage is set by the source and the characteristic impedance; at the load the wave is partly reflected, and the load voltage is the sum of the incident and reflected voltages until the reflection from the source end returns.

steps.description: characteristic impedance of the cable
steps.principle: Characteristic impedance of a lossless line: Z0 = sqrt(L'/C') with L' and C' per unit length, which equals sqrt(L_total/C_total) because the length cancels
steps.why: The line is uniform, so the inductance and capacitance per metre are the totals divided by the same length, and the ratio of the two is the ratio of the totals.

steps.description: reflection coefficient at the load
steps.principle: Reflection coefficient at a resistive load: Gamma = (RL - Z0)/(RL + Z0)
steps.why: The load imposes V = RL I on the sum of the incident and reflected waves, which fixes the fraction of the incident wave that is reflected.

steps.description: voltage of the wave launched into the cable
steps.principle: The source and the line form a voltage divider at the instant of switching: the launched wave has voltage Vs Z0/(Rs + Z0)
steps.why: Before any reflection returns the source sees only the line, which acts like a resistor Z0, so the launched voltage is the divider fraction of the emf.

steps.description: voltage across the load after the first arrival

steps.why: Until the reflection from the source end arrives, the voltage across the load is the sum of the first incident wave and the wave reflected from the load.

steps.description: characteristic impedance of the cable
steps.principle: Characteristic impedance of a lossless line: Z0 = sqrt(L'/C') with L' and C' per unit length, which equals sqrt(L_total/C_total) because the length cancels

steps.description: reflection coefficient at the load
steps.principle: Reflection coefficient at a resistive load: Gamma = (RL - Z0)/(RL + Z0)

steps.description: voltage of the wave launched into the cable

steps.why: Before any reflection returns the source sees only the line, which acts like a resistor Z0, so the launched voltage is the divider fraction of the emf.

steps.description: reflection coefficient at the load
steps.principle: Reflection coefficient at a resistive load: Gamma = (RL - Z0)/(RL + Z0)
steps.why: The load imposes V = RL I on the sum of the incident and reflected waves, which fixes the fraction of the incident wave that is reflected.

steps.description: voltage of the wave launched into the cable

steps.description: voltage across the load after the first arrival

items: The inductor and the wires have no resistance and the capacitors are ideal, so the oscillation continues without loss.

The capacitors are joined with their positive plates together through the inductor and the switch and their negative plates together by a wire, so the charges on the joined plates add, and there is no current in the inductor when the switch closes.

steps.text: Charge moves between the capacitors through the inductor like a mass on a spring: the voltage on the second capacitor oscillates about the balance value, starting from its initial value at rest, so it overshoots the balance value by as much as it started below it.

steps.description: total charge on the two joined plates
steps.principle: Charge conservation for the joined plates: the total charge is Q = C1 V0 + C2 V2
steps.why: The positive plates are joined, so their charges add, and with no resistance this total is conserved as charge moves between the capacitors.

steps.description: common voltage at which the capacitors would balance
steps.principle: Common voltage at balance: with both capacitors at the same voltage the total charge is shared in proportion to capacitance, so the balance voltage is Q/(C1 + C2)
steps.why: At the balance point, where no net voltage drives the current, the two capacitors have equal voltages and hold the conserved total charge, which fixes the centre of the oscillation.

steps.description: largest voltage across the second capacitor
steps.principle: Simple harmonic oscillation from rest: the voltage on the second capacitor is Veq + (V2 - Veq) cos(w t), so its largest value is Veq + (Veq - V2) = 2 Veq - V2
steps.why: The loop equation L q2'' = (Q - q2)/C1 - q2/C2 has the balance charge as its equilibrium; the current is zero at the start, so the voltage swings from V2 to the mirror value on the other side of Veq, and the inductance sets only the period.

steps.text: The largest voltage is independent of the inductance; if the second capacitor started at the balance voltage nothing would move and the formula gives Veq, and as C2 goes to zero the largest voltage approaches 2 V0.
largest voltage across the second capacitor: 148 V

The added sentence ("The inductor has an inductance of 30 mH.") gives the inductance of the coil, q = 30 mH (= 0.03 in SI). It belongs to the system, so it may enter intermediate relations; only the final answer must not depend on it.
Relation 1 that contains q: angular frequency of the transfer w = sqrt((C1 + C2) / (L C1 C2)).
Relation 2 that contains q: voltage on the second capacitor v2(t) = Veq + (V2 - Veq) cos w t.
Relation 3 that contains q: first maximum at t = pi / w, where w t = pi (the inductance cancels).

Combining them, with q kept: Vmax = Veq + (V2 - Veq)*cos(sqrt((C1 + C2)/(q*C1*C2))*(pi/sqrt((C1 + C2)/(q*C1*C2)))). steps.text: Resolve the weight and the electric force along and normal to the slope. The normal force fixes the friction; the net force along the slope gives the acceleration, and constant acceleration from rest gives the speed.

steps.description: component of weight and electric force along the slope, up the slope positive
steps.principle: Components along the slope: the electric force contributes q E cos(theta) up the slope and the weight contributes m g sin(theta) down it
steps.why: Both forces are resolved onto the line of the slope; the difference is the force that drives the block up before friction is taken into account.

steps.description: normal force of the incline on the block
steps.principle: Equilibrium of forces normal to the incline: N = m g cos(theta) + q E sin(theta)
steps.why: The horizontal field pushes the block into the slope as well as along it, so the component of the electric force normal to the slope adds to the normal component of the weight.

steps.description: kinetic friction force
steps.principle: Kinetic friction: F_f = mu N, directed down the slope while the block slides up
steps.why: The block is sliding, so the friction force has its kinetic magnitude, the coefficient times the normal force.

steps.description: acceleration up the slope
steps.principle: Newton's second law along the slope: a = (F_drive - F_friction)/m
steps.why: The net force along the slope is the driving component minus the friction, and dividing by the mass gives the constant acceleration.

steps.description: speed after sliding the distance
steps.principle: Constant acceleration from rest: v^2 = 2 a s
steps.why: The block starts from rest and accelerates uniformly through the distance s along the slope.

steps.text: Find the force between the plates at the final separation, in mN.

items: The battery stays connected, so the voltage across the plates is the emf at every separation; the battery is ideal.
The plates stay flat and parallel and the gap is air taken as a vacuum; edge effects are neglected, so the capacitance is inversely proportional to the separation.

steps.text: At constant voltage the plate charge changes as the plates separate. The force on one plate is half the charge on the other plate times the field of that other plate's partner, that is half Q E for the total field E between the plates.

steps.description: capacitance at the final separation
steps.principle: Parallel-plate capacitance is inversely proportional to the separation: C = C0 d0/d
steps.why: The area and the dielectric are unchanged, so only the separation changes the capacitance.

steps.description: field between the plates at the final separation
steps.principle: Uniform field between parallel plates: E = V/d
steps.why: The voltage across the plates is the emf and the separation is the final one, so the field is the emf divided by the separation.

steps.description: charge on the plates at the final separation
steps.principle: Definition of capacitance: Q = C V at the battery voltage
steps.why: The battery keeps the voltage equal to its emf, so the charge on the plates at the final separation is C1 V.

steps.description: force that one plate exerts on the other
steps.principle: Force on one plate in the field of the other: F = (1/2) Q E, because the field of the other plate alone is half the total field between the plates
steps.why: The charge on one plate lies in the field produced by the other plate, which is half of E, so the force on it is Q E/2.

steps.text: The same force follows from virtual work, F = (1/2) V^2 |dC/dd| = (1/2) V^2 C0 d0/d1^2; the force falls as the inverse square of the separation at fixed voltage.
force between the plates at the final separation: 3.24 mN

Step 3. Assumptions: The battery stays connected, so the voltage across the plates is the emf at every separation; the battery is ideal. This quantity has no path to the target: the further battery was in series with the battery in an earlier run, which is over; in the stated run the capacitor is connected to its stated battery only. items: The magnetic field is uniform and is the only force on the bead; the motion is non-relativistic and gravity and radiation are neglected.

steps.text: The component of the velocity along the field is constant, and the perpendicular component circles at the cyclotron frequency. The pitch is the constant speed along the field times the time of one turn, which does not depend on the perpendicular speed.

steps.description: angular frequency of the circling
steps.principle: Newton's second law with the Lorentz force for circular motion perpendicular to a uniform field: q v B = m v^2/r gives omega = q B/m
steps.why: The magnetic force on the perpendicular component acts as the centripetal force, and the resulting angular frequency does not depend on the size of that component.

steps.description: time for one complete turn
steps.principle: Period of circular motion: T = 2 pi/omega
steps.why: One complete turn of the projected circular motion takes one period, whatever the radius.

steps.description: pitch of the helix
steps.principle: Uniform motion along the field: the advance in one turn is v_parallel times the time T
steps.why: No force acts along the field, so the bead advances along it at constant speed while it completes one circle.

steps.text: The pitch grows in proportion to the mass and to the speed along the field, and falls as the charge or the field increases; for a very large field the helix becomes tightly wound, and the result is in metres.

Step 2. Given: m = 0.5 g (mass of the bead; given); qc = 5 mC (charge of the bead; given); B = 0.8 T (magnetic field strength; given); vpar = 12 m/s (component of the velocity along the field; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The magnetic field is uniform and is the only force on the bead; the motion is non-relativistic and gravity and radiation are neglected. The component of the velocity perpendicular to the field is not zero, so the path is a helix; the component along the field is constant.
Step 4. Approach: The component of the velocity along the field is constant, and the perpendicular component circles at the cyclotron frequency. The pitch is the constant speed along the field times the time of one turn, which does not depend on the perpendicular speed.
Step 5. Newton's second law with the Lorentz force for circular motion perpendicular to a uniform field: q v B = m v^2/r gives omega = q B/m. The magnetic force on the perpendicular component acts as the centripetal force, and the resulting angular frequency does not depend on the size of that component. wc = qc*B/m  (SI units). wc = (0.005)*(0.8)/(0.0005) = 8 (SI) = 8 rad/s.

Step 7. Uniform motion along the field: the advance in one turn is v_parallel times the time T. No force acts along the field, so the bead advances along it at constant speed while it completes one circle. p = vpar*T  (SI units). p = (12)*(0.7854) = 9.425 (SI) = 9.425 m.
Step 8. Check: The pitch grows in proportion to the mass and to the speed along the field, and falls as the charge or the field increases; for a very large field the helix becomes tightly wound, and the result is in metres.
Step 9. Answer: pitch of the helix: 9.425 m.

items.description: molar gas constant, a stated constant
items.name: R

items: The gas is ideal and is heated slowly at constant pressure.

steps.text: We are asked for the heat needed to warm a diatomic ideal gas at constant pressure when only its translation and rotation are excited. Find the temperature rise, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure from the equipartition of energy, and then the heat from the heat capacity.

steps.description: molar heat capacity at constant pressure of the gas
steps.principle: Equipartition of energy: three translational and two rotational quadratic degrees of freedom give Cv = 5R/2, and Mayer's relation Cp = Cv + R gives Cp = 7R/2
steps.why: The molecules rotate but do not vibrate over this range, so vibration adds no degree of freedom; heating at constant pressure also does work on the piston, which is the extra R.

steps.description: rise of the temperature of the gas
steps.principle: Definition of the temperature change, delta T = T2 - T1
steps.why: The heat needed depends on how far the temperature rises, so we first take the difference of the final and initial temperatures.

steps.description: heat supplied to the gas
steps.principle: Heat at constant pressure, Q = n Cp delta T
steps.why: With the molar heat capacity at constant pressure known, the heat supplied is the amount of gas times Cp times the temperature rise.

steps.text: The heat is larger than the change of internal energy, n (5R/2) delta T, by exactly the work n R delta T done on the piston, and it is 7/5 of the heat needed to warm the same gas at constant volume.
heat supplied to the gas: 3.492 kJ

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the heat supplied to the gas, in kJ.
Step 2. Given: n = 2 mol (amount of gas; given); T1 = 300 K (initial temperature of the gas; given); T2 = 360 K (final temperature of the gas; given); R = 8.314 J/(mol*K) (molar gas constant, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The gas is ideal and is heated slowly at constant pressure. The translational and rotational motions of the molecules are fully excited and the vibrational motion is not excited at any temperature of the heating.
Step 4. Approach: We are asked for the heat needed to warm a diatomic ideal gas at constant pressure when only its translation and rotation are excited. Find the temperature rise, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure from the equipartition of energy, and then the heat from the heat capacity.
Step 5. Equipartition of energy: three translational and two rotational quadratic degrees of freedom give Cv = 5R/2, and Mayer's relation Cp = Cv + R gives Cp = 7R/2. The molecules rotate but do not vibrate over this range, so vibration adds no degree of freedom; heating at constant pressure also does work on the piston, which is the extra R. Cp = 7*R/2  (SI units). Cp = 7*(8.314)/2 = 29.1 (SI) = 29.1 J/(mol*K).

Step 2. Step 4. Approach: For steady radial conduction the heat current through every cylindrical shell is the same, so the temperature falls with the logarithm of the radius. Find the logarithms of the two radius ratios, then the temperature fall to the asked radius.
Step 5. Radial conduction in a cylinder, T falls linearly with ln r, so the inner shell has the weight ln(rm/r1). The thermal resistance of a shell between two radii is proportional to the logarithm of their ratio, so we need that logarithm for the shell from the pipe to the asked radius. a = log(rm/r1)  (SI units). a = log((0.05)/(0.03)) = 0.5108 (SI) = 0.5108.
Step 6. Radial conduction in a cylinder, the thermal resistance of the whole insulation is proportional to ln(r2/r1). The same logarithm for the whole insulation layer gives the total resistance, in the same units as the inner shell. b = log(r2/r1)  (SI units). b = log((0.09)/(0.03)) = 1.099 (SI) = 1.099.
Step 7. Steady heat current through thermal resistances in series, T_in - T(rm) = (T_in - T_out) ln(rm/r1)/ln(r2/r1). The heat current is the same through both shells, so the fraction of the total temperature drop across the inner shell is the ratio of the resistances; the conductivity and the pipe length cancel. dTm = (Tin - Tout)*a/b  (SI units). dTm = ((420) - (300))*(0.5108)/(1.099) = 55.8 (SI) = 55.8 K.
Step 8. Check: The fall is smaller than the full temperature difference and larger than the fall a flat slab would give over the same fraction of the thickness, because the area grows with the radius, so most of the drop is near the pipe.
Step 9. Answer: temperature fall from the pipe surface to the stated radius: 55.8 K.

steps.description: mean energy per mole above the ground level

steps.why: Only the two levels are accessible, so the fraction of the molecules in the excited level is w/(1 + w), and each of them carries the energy dE above the ground level, which is the zero of energy.
