gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the temperature of the bullet after it has stopped, in K.
Step 2. Given: v = 300 m/s (speed of the bullet before the impact; given); f = 0.5 (fraction of the kinetic energy that becomes internal energy of the bullet; given); c = 130 J/(kg*K) (specific heat capacity of the metal of the bullet; given); T0 = 293 K (temperature of the bullet when it was loaded; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The stated fraction of the kinetic energy becomes internal energy of the bullet, shared uniformly through it; the rest goes into the plate. The specific heat capacity of the metal is the stated constant over the temperature range, and the bullet stays solid.
Step 4. The added sentence ("After the loading, sunshine warms the bullet by 17 K before the shot.") gives q = 17 K. Sunshine that has warmed the bullet by q before the shot makes the temperature at the impact T0 + q. In the graph this changes the input T0 (temperature of the bullet when it was loaded): T0' = T0 + q = 293 + 17 = 310 K. Every later step uses the changed T0.
Step 5. Approach: The stated fraction of the kinetic energy of the bullet is turned into internal energy, so the temperature rise follows from the specific heat capacity. Working per unit mass, find the kinetic energy, the temperature rise and the final temperature.
Step 6. Kinetic energy per unit mass, e = v^2/2. The energy that can be turned into heat is the kinetic energy; per unit mass it does not depend on the mass of the bullet. ek = v**2/2  (SI units). ek = (300)**2/2 = 4.5e+04 (SI) = 4.5e+04 J/kg.
Step 7. Heat and temperature rise, Q = m c delta T, with Q = f m v^2/2 the share of the kinetic energy that heats the bullet. Setting the heat taken in by the bullet equal to the stated fraction of its kinetic energy, the mass cancels and the rise is f e/c. dT = f*ek/c  (SI units). dT = (0.5)*(4.5e+04)/(130) = 173.1 (SI) = 173.1 K.
Step 8. Final temperature is the initial temperature plus the rise, T = T0 + delta T. The question asks for the temperature of the bullet, not for its rise, so the initial temperature is added. Tf = T0 + dT  (SI units). Tf = (310) + (173.1) = 483.1 (SI) = 483.1 K.
Step 9. Check: The rise is independent of the mass of the bullet, grows with the square of the speed, and is below the value for f = 1; it is of order a hundred kelvin for a speed of a few hundred metres per second in a soft metal.
Step 10. Answer: temperature of the bullet after it has stopped: 483.1 K.

items.description: speed of sound in the still air, a stated constant
items.name: c

items: The speed of sound has the stated constant value in the still air and does not depend on the frequency.
The wall moves at constant speed along the line to the loudspeaker and reflects the sound straight back with no change of frequency in its own frame; the air is still.

steps.text: The wall is a moving receiver of the tone and then a moving source of the echo, so the Doppler effect acts twice. First find the frequency that the approaching wall receives, then the frequency of the echo that it sends back to the stationary microphone, and finally the difference between the echo and the original tone, which is the beat.

steps.description: frequency of the sound that reaches the wall
steps.principle: Doppler effect for a stationary source and an observer moving towards it at speed v: f1 = f (c + v) / c
steps.why: The wall moves towards the loudspeaker, so it meets the crests more often than they are emitted. Taking the wall as the observer of the stationary source gives the frequency that the wall receives.

steps.description: frequency of the echo at the microphone
steps.principle: Doppler effect for a source (the wall, re-emitting the sound) moving towards a stationary observer: f2 = f1 c / (c - v)
steps.why: The wall re-emits the sound it received at the frequency f1, and as a source moving towards the microphone it crowds the crests together. The combination of the two shifts is f2 = f (c + v) / (c - v).

steps.description: beat frequency between the tone and the echo
steps.principle: Beat frequency of two superposed tones: the difference of their frequencies, f2 - f
steps.why: The microphone records the original tone and the echo together. Two tones of nearby frequencies give an amplitude that oscillates at the difference frequency, which is the beat asked for.

steps.text: Limiting case: for v much smaller than c the beat is about 2 f v / c, and it is zero when the wall is at rest. Order of magnitude: 440 Hz with a wall at 3 m/s gives about 8 Hz. The distance to the wall does not enter at all.
beat frequency between the tone and the echo: 7.765 Hz

Step 3. Assumptions: The speed of sound has the stated constant value in the still air and does not depend on the frequency. The wall moves at constant speed along the line to the loudspeaker and reflects the sound straight back with no change of frequency in its own frame; the air is still.
Step 4. Approach: The wall is a moving receiver of the tone and then a moving source of the echo, so the Doppler effect acts twice. First find the frequency that the approaching wall receives, then the frequency of the echo that it sends back to the stationary microphone, and finally the difference between the echo and the original tone, which is the beat.
Step 5. Doppler effect for a stationary source and an observer moving towards it at speed v: f1 = f (c + v) / c. The wall moves towards the loudspeaker, so it meets the crests more often than they are emitted. Taking the wall as the observer of the stationary source gives the frequency that the wall receives. f1 = f*(c + v)/c  (SI units). f1 = (440)*((343) + (3))/(343) = 443.8 (SI) = 443.8 Hz.

The combination of the two shifts is f2 = f (c + v) / (c - v). f2 = f1*c/(c - v)  (SI units). f2 = (443.8)*(343)/((343) - (3)) = 447.8 (SI) = 447.8 Hz.
Step 7. Beat frequency of two superposed tones: the difference of their frequencies, f2 - f. The microphone records the original tone and the echo together. Two tones of nearby frequencies give an amplitude that oscillates at the difference frequency, which is the beat asked for. beat = f2 - f  (SI units). beat = (447.8) - (440) = 7.765 (SI) = 7.765 Hz.
Step 8. Check: Limiting case: for v much smaller than c the beat is about 2 f v / c, and it is zero when the wall is at rest. Order of magnitude: 440 Hz with a wall at 3 m/s gives about 8 Hz. The distance to the wall does not enter at all.

steps.description: Fresnel amplitude reflection coefficient for p-polarised light

steps.text: The added sentence ("An optical amplifier adds 3.4 mW to the power of the beam.") gives q = 3.4 mW. An optical amplifier that adds q to the power of the beam, whose stated power is the power at the laser, makes the incident power P0 + q, and the transmitted power is (P0 + q) (1 - R). In the graph this changes the input P0 (power of the incident beam): P0' = P0 + q = 5 + 3.4 = 8.4 mW. Every later step uses the changed P0.

At oblique incidence the reflected fraction of a p-polarised beam depends on the angle, so use Snell's law for the angle in the glass, the Fresnel amplitude coefficient for p-polarisation, then the reflected fraction of the power; the rest enters the glass.

steps.description: angle of refraction in the glass
steps.principle: Snell's law, sin(theta_t) = sin(theta) / n
steps.why: The Fresnel coefficient needs the angle of the refracted ray in the glass, and the light goes from air, of index one, into the glass of index n.

steps.description: Fresnel amplitude reflection coefficient for p-polarised light
steps.principle: Fresnel equation for the amplitude reflection coefficient of p-polarised light, r_p = (n cos(theta) - cos(theta_t)) / (n cos(theta) + cos(theta_t))

steps.description: fraction of the power that is reflected

steps.why: The power carried by a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude, and the incident and reflected waves are in the same medium, so the reflected fraction of the power is r_p squared.

steps.description: power that enters the glass

steps.why: The glass does not absorb light and only the first surface is considered, so whatever is not reflected enters the glass; this is the power asked for.

Step 2. Given: eta = 0.4 Pa*s (dynamic viscosity of the oil; given); L = 10 cm (length of the rotor; given); R1 = 20 mm (radius of the rotor; given); R2 = 22 mm (inner radius of the fixed cylinder; given); rot = 120 rpm (rotation rate of the rotor; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The oil is Newtonian and sticks to both surfaces, its flow is steady, laminar and purely azimuthal, and end effects are neglected. The rotation rate in revolutions per minute is converted to the angular velocity omega = 2 pi rot / 60.
Step 4. Approach: In the narrow gap the oil shears; the torque that the rotor must overcome is fixed by the viscosity and the velocity profile between the cylinders. Find the angular velocity, the viscous torque for steady laminar flow, then the power.
Step 5. Conversion of the rotation rate, omega = 2 pi N / 60. The viscous torque is written with the angular velocity in radians per second, so the rotation rate in revolutions per minute is converted first. omega = rot  (SI units). omega = (12.57) = 12.57 (SI) = 12.57 rad/s.
Step 6. Viscous shear stress tau = eta r d(omega)/dr in steady azimuthal flow gives the torque T = 4 pi eta L omega R1^2 R2^2 / (R2^2 - R1^2). The torque transmitted through every cylindrical layer of oil is the same, so tau 2 pi r L r is constant and the angular velocity falls as 1 / r^2 between the sticking surfaces of the rotor and the outer cylinder. Fitting the boundary values omega at R1 and zero at R2 gives the torque. T = 4*pi*eta*L*omega*R1**2*R2**2/(R2**2 - R1**2)  (SI units). T = 4*pi*(0.4)*(0.1)*(12.57)*(0.02)**2*(0.022)**2/((0.022)**2 - (0.02)**2) = 0.01456 (SI) = 0.01456 N*m.
Step 7. Power of a torque turning at angular velocity omega, P = T omega. The rotor turns steadily, so the driving power equals the rate at which the viscous torque is overcome. P = T*omega  (SI units). P = (0.01456)*(12.57) = 0.1829 (SI) = 0.1829 W.
Step 8. Check: Limiting case: for a narrow gap the torque reduces to 2 pi eta L omega R^3 / (gap), the plane Couette result. The power grows as the square of the rotation rate and in proportion to the viscosity and length.
Step 9. Answer: power needed to turn the rotor: 0.1829 W.

A retarder rotated against the polarisation splits the light into two components, delays one of them by a phase difference, and the crossed analyser makes them interfere. Find the phase difference, its interference factor, then the power.

steps.description: phase difference between the two axes
steps.principle: Phase difference accumulated across a birefringent plate, delta = 2 pi dn d / lambda
steps.why: The slow axis has the higher index, so the light along it is delayed by dn d over the plate; in units of the wavelength this gives the phase difference.

steps.description: factor sin^2 of half the phase difference
steps.principle: Interference factor of two equal-amplitude components, sin^2(delta / 2)
steps.why: The analyser projects the two components onto the y axis, where they have equal and opposite signs; their phase difference delta makes the sum of their fields proportional to sin(delta / 2).

steps.description: power that passes the analyser
steps.principle: Jones calculus for a rotated retarder between crossed polarisers, P = P0 sin^2(2 alpha) sin^2(delta / 2)
steps.why: The component of the x-polarised field along each axis is cos(alpha) and sin(alpha); projecting both on y and adding with the phase difference gives an amplitude sin(2 alpha) sin(delta / 2), so the power is its square times P0.

steps.text: Limiting cases: with the axis along x or y (alpha zero or ninety degrees) nothing passes, and with a phase difference of pi (a half-wave plate) at forty-five degrees all of the power passes. The result never exceeds P0.
power that passes the analyser: 5.12 mW

steps.text: Find the absolute pressure of the liquid at the highest point, in kPa.

items.description: height of the highest point above the reservoir surface
items.name: H

items.description: depth of the outlet below the reservoir surface
items.name: h

items: g is a uniform constant of the stated value.
The liquid is incompressible and flows steadily without friction through a tube of uniform bore that stays full, and the reservoir is so large that its level does not fall.
The surface of the reservoir and the outlet are both open to the atmosphere at the stated pressure.

steps.text: The liquid flows at the speed set by the drop to the outlet, and at the highest point its pressure is the atmospheric pressure minus the pressure needed to lift the liquid and to give it kinetic energy. Find the speed first, then the dynamic pressure, then Bernoulli's equation to the highest point.

steps.description: speed of the liquid in the tube
steps.principle: Bernoulli's equation between the reservoir surface and the open outlet, both at atmospheric pressure: v = sqrt(2 g h)
steps.why: The reservoir is large, so the surface speed is zero, and both ends are at atmospheric pressure, so the whole drop h of the outlet below the surface goes into kinetic energy. The speed of the liquid is the same everywhere in a tube of uniform bore.

steps.description: dynamic pressure of the moving liquid
steps.principle: Dynamic pressure of a moving liquid, rho v^2 / 2
steps.why: At the highest point the liquid moves at the same speed, so part of its energy per volume is kinetic, and the pressure falls by this amount in addition to the hydrostatic part.

steps.description: absolute pressure of the liquid at the highest point
steps.principle: Bernoulli's equation between the surface and the highest point, p0 = p_c + rho g H + rho v^2 / 2

steps.text: The current is the number of electrons collected per second times the elementary charge. Find the energy of one photon, then how many photons arrive per second, then multiply by the probability that a photon releases an electron.

steps.description: energy of one photon of the light
steps.principle: Planck-Einstein relation, E = h c / lambda, with hc given in eV nm
steps.why: Light of one wavelength comes in photons of the same energy, and with hc in eV nm and the wavelength in nm the energy comes out in electron volts.

steps.principle: Current as charge per second, I = eta e N_dot, with every released electron collected
steps.why: A fraction eta of the photons releases one electron each, and the anode voltage is high enough to collect all of them, so the current is the electron rate times the elementary charge.

steps.text: Order of magnitude: one milliwatt of visible light is about 10^15 to 10^16 photons per second, and a probability of a few tenths of a percent gives microamperes. The current is proportional to the power and to the wavelength.

Step 3. Assumptions: The anode voltage is high enough that every released electron is collected, so the current does not depend on it. steps.why: The activity of each isotope falls as exp(-lambda t), and the half-life is the time in which it falls to one half, so the decay constant of isotope 1 follows from its half-life.

Step 2. Given: A1 = 2400 Bq (activity of isotope 1 at the moment of preparation; given); A2 = 500 Bq (activity of isotope 2 at the moment of preparation; given); T1 = 6 h (half-life of isotope 1; given); T2 = 72 h (half-life of isotope 2; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The two isotopes decay independently: neither is produced by the decay of the other, and each decays by the exponential law from its stated initial activity. The counter detects a decay of either isotope with the same efficiency, which does not change in time, so the count rates are in the ratio of the activities.
Step 4. The added sentence ("At the moment of preparation, a further 170 Bq batch of the longer-lived isotope is added to the sample.") gives q = 170 Bq. A further batch of the longer-lived isotope, added at the moment of preparation, makes its activity A2 + q, so the count rates cross earlier. In the graph this changes the input A2 (activity of isotope 2 at the moment of preparation): A2' = A2 + q = 500 + 170 = 670 Bq. Every later step uses the changed A2.
Step 5. Approach: Each isotope's count rate is proportional to its activity, and the counter has the same efficiency for both, so the count rates are equal exactly when the activities are equal. Find the two decay constants and solve for the time at which the exponentially falling activities cross.
Step 6. Relation between half-life and decay constant, lambda = ln 2 / T_half. The activity of each isotope falls as exp(-lambda t), and the half-life is the time in which it falls to one half, so the decay constant of isotope 1 follows from its half-life. lam1 = log(2)/T1  (SI units). lam1 = log(2)/(2.16e+04) = 3.209e-05 (SI) = 3.209e-05 1/s.
Step 7. Relation between half-life and decay constant, lambda = ln 2 / T_half. The same relation gives the decay constant of isotope 2, which is smaller because its half-life is longer. lam2 = log(2)/T2  (SI units). lam2 = log(2)/(2.592e+05) = 2.674e-06 (SI) = 2.674e-06 1/s.
Step 8. Exponential decay of each activity, A_i exp(-lambda_i t), set equal: A1 exp(-lam1 t) = A2 exp(-lam2 t). Equal count rates mean equal activities. Taking logarithms gives ln(A1 / A2) = (lam1 - lam2) t, so the time is ln(A1 / A2) divided by the difference of the decay constants. t = log(A1/A2)/(lam1 - lam2)  (SI units). t = log((2400)/(670))/((3.209e-05) - (2.674e-06)) = 4.338e+04 (SI) = 12.05 h.
Step 9. Check: Limiting cases: if the two activities started equal the time would be zero, and the time grows only logarithmically with the ratio of the activities. It must be positive, because the short-lived isotope starts higher and falls faster.
Step 10. Answer: time at which the two count rates are equal: 12.05 h.

steps.description: sine of half the scattering angle
steps.principle: Half the scattering angle, sin(theta / 2)
steps.why: For a Coulomb orbit the closest approach and the impact parameter are fixed by the deflection through the sine and cotangent of half the scattering angle.

steps.description: distance of closest approach in a head-on collision
steps.principle: Energy conservation for a head-on collision, K = (2 e)(Z e) / (4 pi eps0 D), so D = 2 Z e^2 / (4 pi eps0 K)

steps.description: distance of closest approach of the scattered alpha particle

steps.text: Limiting cases: for theta = 180 degrees the result equals D, the head-on value, and for small angles it grows without bound as the alpha particle passes far from the nucleus. The result must exceed D / 2, and falls as the energy rises.

Step 3. Assumptions: The force between an alpha particle and a nucleus is purely electrostatic between point charges 2e and Ze. Step 4. The added sentence ("For this scattering, an extra accelerating stage gives 3 MeV more kinetic energy to each alpha particle on its way to the foil.") gives q = 3 MeV. A further accelerating gap that adds q to the kinetic energy of the alpha particles before the foil makes it K + q, and the head-on closest approach, and so the closest approach, falls. In the graph this changes the input K (kinetic energy of an alpha particle when it leaves the source): K' = K + q = 5 + 3 = 8 MeV. Every later step uses the changed K.
Step 5. Approach: The alpha particle moves in the Coulomb field of the nucleus, which stays at rest. Find the head-on closest approach from energy conservation, then the closest approach for the stated deflection from the geometry of the hyperbolic orbit.
Step 6. Coulomb constant times the elementary charge squared, e^2 / (4 pi eps0). steps.description: sine of half the scattering angle
steps.principle: Half the scattering angle, sin(theta / 2)
steps.why: For a Coulomb orbit the closest approach and the impact parameter are fixed by the deflection through the sine and cotangent of half the scattering angle.

steps.description: distance of closest approach in a head-on collision
steps.principle: Energy conservation for a head-on collision, K = (2 e)(Z e) / (4 pi eps0 D), so D = 2 Z e^2 / (4 pi eps0 K)

steps.description: distance of closest approach of the scattered alpha particle

steps.why: Energy and angular momentum conservation at the turning point give r^2 - D r - b^2 = 0, with the impact parameter b = (D / 2) cot(theta / 2); its positive root is the closest approach, which reduces to D for a deflection of 180 degrees.

steps.text: Limiting cases: for theta = 180 degrees the result equals D, the head-on value, and for small angles it grows without bound as the alpha particle passes far from the nucleus. The result must exceed D / 2, and falls as the energy rises.

Step 2. Given: Z = 79 (number of protons in a nucleus of the foil; given); K = 5 MeV (kinetic energy of an alpha particle when it leaves the source; given); theta = 90 deg (angle through which the alpha particle is scattered; given); e = 1.602e-19 C (elementary charge, a stated constant; stated constant); eps0 = 8.854e-12 F/m (permittivity of free space, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The force between an alpha particle and a nucleus is purely electrostatic between point charges 2e and Ze. The nucleus is much heavier than the alpha particle and stays at rest, and each alpha particle is scattered only once, by a single nucleus. e and eps0 are the stated constants, and the motion is non-relativistic.
Step 4. The added sentence ("A further accelerating gap adds 3.6 MeV to the kinetic energy of the alpha particles from the source before they are directed at their targets.") gives q = 3.6 MeV. A further accelerating gap that adds q to the kinetic energy of the alpha particles before the foil makes it K + q, and the head-on closest approach, and so the closest approach, falls. In the graph this changes the input K (kinetic energy of an alpha particle when it leaves the source): K' = K + q = 5 + 3.6 = 8.6 MeV. Every later step uses the changed K.
Step 5. Approach: The alpha particle moves in the Coulomb field of the nucleus, which stays at rest. Find the head-on closest approach from energy conservation, then the closest approach for the stated deflection from the geometry of the hyperbolic orbit.
Step 6. Coulomb constant times the elementary charge squared, e^2 / (4 pi eps0). The nucleus is much heavier than the alpha particle and stays at rest, and each alpha particle is scattered only once, by a single nucleus.
e and eps0 are the stated constants, and the motion is non-relativistic.

steps.text: The added sentence ("A separate nucleus B in another foil has a closest approach of 0.05492 pm, but it is unrelated to this nucleus.") gives 0.05492 pm. This quantity has no path to the target: it describes another system B in a convertible unit; it is not an input of any relation of this problem and equals the answer's magnitude only by construction. It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.

The alpha particle moves in the Coulomb field of the nucleus, which stays at rest. Find the head-on closest approach from energy conservation, then the closest approach for the stated deflection from the geometry of the hyperbolic orbit.

steps.description: Coulomb constant times the elementary charge squared
steps.principle: Coulomb constant times the elementary charge squared, e^2 / (4 pi eps0)
steps.why: The electrostatic potential energy of two point charges is the product of the charges times e^2 / (4 pi eps0) / r, and this combination, in eV nm, is the unit in which the potential energy is easiest to compare with a kinetic energy.

steps.description: sine of half the scattering angle
steps.principle: Half the scattering angle, sin(theta / 2)
steps.why: For a Coulomb orbit the closest approach and the impact parameter are fixed by the deflection through the sine and cotangent of half the scattering angle.

steps.description: distance of closest approach in a head-on collision
steps.principle: Energy conservation for a head-on collision, K = (2 e)(Z e) / (4 pi eps0 D), so D = 2 Z e^2 / (4 pi eps0 K)
steps.why: In a head-on collision the alpha particle stops where its whole kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy; this distance D is the largest possible closest approach scale of the orbit.

steps.description: distance of closest approach of the scattered alpha particle
steps.principle: Closest approach on the hyperbolic Rutherford orbit, d = (D / 2)(1 + 1 / sin(theta / 2))
steps.why: Energy and angular momentum conservation at the turning point give r^2 - D r - b^2 = 0, with the impact parameter b = (D / 2) cot(theta / 2); its positive root is the closest approach, which reduces to D for a deflection of 180 degrees.

steps.text: Limiting cases: for theta = 180 degrees the result equals D, the head-on value, and for small angles it grows without bound as the alpha particle passes far from the nucleus. The result must exceed D / 2, and falls as the energy rises.
distance of closest approach: 54.92 fm

Step 3. Assumptions: The force between an alpha particle and a nucleus is purely electrostatic between point charges 2e and Ze. The nucleus is much heavier than the alpha particle and stays at rest, and each alpha particle is scattered only once, by a single nucleus. e and eps0 are the stated constants, and the motion is non-relativistic.
Step 4. The added sentence ("A separate nucleus B in another foil has a closest approach of 0.05492 pm, but it is unrelated to this nucleus.") gives 0.05492 pm. steps.text: Treat the positron and the electron as one system with a definite total energy and momentum, and share these between the two photons, one forward and one backward, using conservation of energy and of momentum along the line of motion.

steps.description: total energy of the positron and the electron
steps.principle: Energy of the system, the kinetic energy plus the rest energies of the positron and of the electron, K + 2 m c^2
steps.why: The electron is at rest and has only its rest energy, and the positron has its rest energy plus its kinetic energy.

steps.description: momentum of the positron times the speed of light
steps.principle: Relativistic energy-momentum relation, (K + m c^2)^2 = (pc)^2 + (m c^2)^2, so pc = sqrt(K^2 + 2 K m c^2)
steps.why: Only the positron moves, so the total momentum of the system is the momentum of the positron.

steps.description: energy of the photon that travels forward
steps.principle: Conservation of energy and of momentum for two collinear photons, E_f + E_b = E_tot and E_f - E_b = pc
steps.why: Photons carry momentum equal to their energy over c, forward positive and backward negative; solving the two equations gives the forward energy as half the sum of the total energy and pc.

steps.text: Limiting case: with no kinetic energy the photons share the energy equally, 511 keV each. The forward photon always carries more than the backward one, and the two energies add to the total energy and differ by pc.
energy of the forward photon: 1515 keV

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the energy of the forward photon, in keV.
Step 2. Given: K = 800 keV (kinetic energy of the positron when it leaves the source; given); mc2 = 511 keV (rest energy of the electron and of the positron, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The electron is free and at rest, and the positron and the electron annihilate into exactly two photons. The two photons are emitted along the line of motion of the positron, one forward and one backward. The rest energies of the electron and the positron are the stated constant.
Step 4. Approach: Treat the positron and the electron as one system with a definite total energy and momentum, and share these between the two photons, one forward and one backward, using conservation of energy and of momentum along the line of motion.
Step 5. Energy of the system, the kinetic energy plus the rest energies of the positron and of the electron, K + 2 m c^2. The electron is at rest and has only its rest energy, and the positron has its rest energy plus its kinetic energy. Etot = K + 2*mc2  (SI units). Etot = (1.282e-13) + 2*(8.187e-14) = 2.919e-13 (SI) = 1822 keV.
Step 6. Relativistic energy-momentum relation, (K + m c^2)^2 = (pc)^2 + (m c^2)^2, so pc = sqrt(K^2 + 2 K m c^2). Only the positron moves, so the total momentum of the system is the momentum of the positron. pc = sqrt(K**2 + 2*K*mc2)  (SI units). pc = sqrt((1.282e-13)**2 + 2*(1.282e-13)*(8.187e-14)) = 1.934e-13 (SI) = 1207 keV.
Step 7. Conservation of energy and of momentum for two collinear photons, E_f + E_b = E_tot and E_f - E_b = pc. Photons carry momentum equal to their energy over c, forward positive and backward negative; solving the two equations gives the forward energy as half the sum of the total energy and pc. Ef = (Etot + pc)/2  (SI units). Ef = ((2.919e-13) + (1.934e-13))/2 = 2.427e-13 (SI) = 1515 keV.
Step 8. Check: Limiting case: with no kinetic energy the photons share the energy equally, 511 keV each. The forward photon always carries more than the backward one, and the two energies add to the total energy and differ by pc.
Step 9. Answer: energy of the forward photon: 1515 keV.

steps.text: Find the number of photons absorbed before the atom stops, in 1.

items.description: kinetic energy of one atom when it enters the laser beam
items.name: K

items: The laser light is directed against the motion of the atoms and its frequency is swept so that each atom stays in resonance and keeps absorbing photons until it has stopped.
Each absorbed photon is re-emitted in a random direction, so the recoil of the emitted photons averages to zero; the speed is small enough for the motion to be non-relativistic.
h is the stated constant.

steps.text: Each absorbed photon changes the momentum of the atom by the momentum of the photon, opposite to its motion; the emitted photons recoil in random directions and average to zero. Divide the initial speed, found from the kinetic energy, by the change of speed per absorption.

steps.description: momentum of one photon of the laser light
steps.principle: Momentum of a photon, p = h / lambda
steps.why: Light of wavelength lambda is made of photons that each carry the momentum h / lambda along the beam, and this is the momentum that an absorbing atom takes up.

steps.description: speed of the atoms when they enter the laser beam
steps.principle: Non-relativistic kinetic energy, K = M v0^2 / 2, so v0 = sqrt(2 K / M)
steps.why: The atoms are slow compared with the speed of light, so their speed follows from the kinetic energy and the mass, with the energy converted from electron volts to joules and the mass from atomic mass units to kilograms.

steps.description: decrease of the speed of the atom in one absorption
steps.principle: Conservation of momentum in one absorption, M dv = p, so dv = p / M
steps.why: The atom absorbs the photon completely, so the momentum that it gains is the photon momentum, directed against the atom's velocity, and its speed falls by p / M; the non-relativistic relation is accurate for these speeds.

steps.description: number of photons that the atom absorbs before it stops
steps.principle: Repeated absorption, N dv = v0, so N = v0 / dv
steps.why: The speed falls by the same amount in each absorption because the emitted photons average to zero recoil, so the number of absorptions that stops the atom is the initial speed divided by the decrease per absorption.

steps.text: Order of magnitude: a sodium atom at several hundred metres per second loses about three centimetres per second per absorption, so it needs tens of thousands of photons. The number scales with the square root of the kinetic energy and the mass and inversely with the photon momentum.
number of photons absorbed before the atom stops: 2.716e+04 1

steps.why: The intensity behind the shield must be smaller than the unshielded intensity by the factor F, so the total exponent mu_c t_c + mu_pb t_pb must equal ln(F).

steps.principle: Exponential attenuation, I = I0 exp(-mu x), applied to the concrete: exponent mu_c t_c

steps.principle: Additivity of the exponents of successive layers, mu_pb t_pb = L - x_c
steps.why: The concrete already supplies x_c of the required exponent, so the lead must supply the difference, which divided by mu_pb is the thickness of the sheet.

steps.text: The added sentence ("For an earlier shield, the builders laid a little more concrete against its wall.") contains no number: there is no quantity to use, so the problem is the base problem.

The intensity of a narrow beam falls exponentially with the thickness of each material, so the exponents add. Find the exponent that the whole shield must supply, subtract the exponent of the concrete, and divide the rest by the coefficient of lead.

steps.description: attenuation exponent that the whole shield must provide
steps.principle: Required attenuation, I / I0 = 1 / F, so the whole shield needs the exponent ln(F)
steps.why: The intensity behind the shield must be smaller than the unshielded intensity by the factor F, so the total exponent mu_c t_c + mu_pb t_pb must equal ln(F).

steps.description: attenuation exponent of the concrete wall
steps.principle: Exponential attenuation, I = I0 exp(-mu x), applied to the concrete: exponent mu_c t_c
steps.why: The concrete wall reduces the intensity by the factor exp(-mu_c t_c); its exponent is the product of the coefficient and the thickness, with the thickness in metres.

steps.description: thickness of the lead sheet
steps.principle: Additivity of the exponents of successive layers, mu_pb t_pb = L - x_c
steps.why: The concrete already supplies x_c of the required exponent, so the lead must supply the difference, which divided by mu_pb is the thickness of the sheet.

steps.text: Limiting cases: a wall that already supplies the whole exponent needs no lead, and a thicker wall needs a thinner sheet. The source intensity does not appear, because only the ratio of the intensities is fixed.
thickness of the lead sheet: 5.888 cm

steps.text: Light carries momentum, with a flux equal to its intensity over c. The mirror receives the normal part of the momentum that it absorbs, and twice that part for the light that it reflects. Find the pressure, then the force on the whole mirror, then the acceleration, and integrate it over the time.

steps.description: geometric and reflection factor of the normal momentum transfer
steps.principle: Normal momentum transfer per unit area for a reflectivity Rf: absorbed (1 - Rf) plus reflected 2 Rf, so (1 + Rf), times cos^2(theta) from the oblique incidence
steps.why: The beam's momentum flux per unit area of the mirror is I cos(theta) / c, and only its normal component, a further factor cos(theta), is transferred to the mirror, so the geometry gives cos^2(theta); the reflected part reverses the normal component, which doubles its transfer.

steps.description: radiation pressure of this beam on a perfectly absorbing surface perpendicular to it
steps.principle: Momentum flux of a beam of intensity I, I / c
steps.why: A beam of intensity I carries I / c of momentum per unit area per second along its direction; this is the pressure on a perfectly absorbing surface perpendicular to the beam.

steps.description: radiation pressure on the mirror, normal to its surface
steps.principle: Radiation pressure on the mirror, p = (1 + Rf) cos^2(theta) I / c
steps.why: Multiplying the pressure on a perfect absorber by the combined reflection and geometry factor gives the normal pressure on the partly reflecting mirror.

steps.description: normal force of the light on the mirror
steps.principle: Force from a pressure on an area, F = p A
steps.why: The beam illuminates the whole mirror, so the pressure acts on its full area, and the normal force is the product.

steps.description: acceleration of the mirror along its rail
steps.principle: Newton's second law along the rail, a = F / m
steps.why: The rail is frictionless and normal to the mirror, so the normal force is the only force along it and the acceleration is constant.

steps.principle: Kinematics of constant acceleration from rest, v = a t
steps.why: The mirror starts at rest and its speed stays far below c, so the force does not change and the speed is the acceleration times the time, with the time converted to seconds.

steps.text: A magnetic moment in a field feels a torque, and because it is tied to the spin angular momentum, the spin precesses about the field. The angular frequency of the precession is the gyromagnetic ratio times the field.

The added sentence ("The spin of the proton is inclined at 43° to the field.") gives the angle between the spin and the field, q = 43 deg (= 0.7505 in SI). It belongs to the system, so it may enter intermediate relations; only the final answer must not depend on it.
Relation 1 that contains q: torque on the moment, mu B sin(q), with mu = (g e / 2 m) L.
Relation 2 that contains q: component of the spin angular momentum perpendicular to the field, L sin(q).
Relation 3 that contains q: precession angular frequency = torque / perpendicular angular momentum.
q cancels: the expression simplifies to B*e*gp/(4*pi*mp), and its derivative with respect to q is 0. The answer is the same for every q: 14.9 MHz.
Order of magnitude: for a proton the frequency is about 42.6 MHz per tesla, so a field of a third of a tesla gives about 15 MHz. The frequency is proportional to the field.
precession frequency of the proton spin: 14.9 MHz

steps.description: Lorentz factor of the proton
steps.principle: Relativistic kinetic energy, K = (gamma - 1) m c^2, so gamma = 1 + K / (m c^2)
steps.why: The kinetic energy is the total energy minus the rest energy, and gamma is the ratio of the total energy to the rest energy.

steps.description: angular frequency of the orbit
steps.principle: Circular motion in a magnetic field with the relativistic momentum, gamma m v = e B r, so w = v / r = e B / (gamma m)
steps.why: The magnetic force e v B is perpendicular to the velocity and supplies the centripetal force on the momentum gamma m v; the speed cancels from the angular frequency, which depends on the energy only through gamma.

steps.description: orbital frequency of the proton
steps.principle: Relation between angular frequency and frequency, f = w / (2 pi)
steps.why: The orbital frequency is the number of revolutions per second, the angular frequency over 2 pi.

steps.description: glancing angle of the first-order Bragg reflection
steps.principle: Bragg's law for the first order, 2 d sin(theta) = lambda
steps.why: Waves reflected from successive planes interfere constructively when the path difference, 2 d sin(theta), is one wavelength; the angle is measured from the planes.

steps.text: Limiting cases: for a kinetic energy small compared with 511 keV the relation reduces to lambda = h / sqrt(2 m K), and the angle falls as the energy rises. The argument of the arcsine must be below one, which it is here by a wide margin.

Step 2. Step 3. Assumptions: The momentum of the electron is the relativistic momentum, so that (pc)^2 = K^2 + 2 K mc^2, and the de Broglie wavelength is hc / (pc). The first-order reflection from a single family of parallel lattice planes obeys Bragg's law with the stated spacing, and the glancing angle is measured from the planes. hc and the electron rest energy are the stated constants.
Step 4. The added sentence ("A separate crystal B in another laboratory reflects at 0.04327 rad, but it is unrelated to this crystal.") gives 0.04327 rad. This quantity has no path to the target: it describes another system B in a convertible unit; it is not an input of any relation of this problem and equals the answer's magnitude only by construction. steps.text: The probe moves only under the pull of the moon, so its total energy per unit mass is conserved. Find the total energy from the launch speed and the potential at the surface, then the distance at which the kinetic energy is zero, then subtract the radius.

steps.description: kinetic energy per unit mass at the launch
steps.principle: Kinetic energy per unit mass, e = v^2/2
steps.why: The launch speed fixes the kinetic energy per unit mass, which does not depend on the mass of the probe.

steps.description: total energy per unit mass of the probe
steps.principle: Total energy per unit mass in an inverse-square field, e = v^2/2 - g0 R (the potential at the surface is -G M/R = -g0 R)
steps.why: The pull of the moon is conservative, so the kinetic energy at launch plus the potential at the surface is the total energy of the probe.

steps.description: distance of the highest point from the centre of the moon
steps.principle: Energy conservation at the highest point, where the speed is zero: e = -G M/r_max = -g0 R^2/r_max
steps.why: At the highest point only the potential energy remains, so the negative total energy fixes the distance from the centre of the moon.

steps.description: greatest height above the surface
steps.principle: Height is distance from the centre minus the radius of the moon, H = r_max - R
steps.why: The question asks for the height above the surface, not the distance from the centre.

steps.text: The height is larger than the flat-field value v^2/(2 g0), which would hold if the pull did not weaken with height, and it grows without limit as the launch speed approaches the escape speed.
greatest height above the surface: 1157 km

The work of the engines equals the change of the total mechanical energy of the satellite. For a circular orbit the total energy is minus the kinetic energy. Find the two orbit radii and the difference of the two total energies.

steps.description: radius of the initial orbit
steps.principle: Radius of a circular orbit, r = R_E + altitude
steps.why: The altitude is measured from the surface, while the law of gravity needs the distance from the centre of the Earth.

steps.description: radius of the final orbit
steps.principle: Radius of a circular orbit, r = R_E + altitude
steps.why: The final orbit is treated in the same way as the initial orbit.

steps.description: work done by the engines
steps.principle: Work-energy theorem with the total energy of a circular orbit, E = -G M m/(2 r) = -m g0 R^2/(2 r)
steps.why: The engines supply the change of the total energy; for a circular orbit the centripetal condition makes the kinetic energy half of the magnitude of the potential energy, so E is minus the kinetic energy.

steps.text: The work is positive and is less than the change of the potential energy alone, because the kinetic energy decreases as the satellite goes up; it vanishes when the two altitudes are equal.
work done by the engines: 2.638e+06 kJ

gold_trace.text:
Step 1. Find the work done by the engines, in kJ.
Step 2. Given: m = 850 kg (mass of the satellite; given); g0 = 9.8 m/s² (gravitational acceleration at the surface of the Earth, a stated constant; stated constant); Re = 6371 km (radius of the Earth, a stated constant; stated constant); h1 = 400 km (altitude of the initial circular orbit; given); h2 = 1200 km (altitude of the final circular orbit; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The Earth is a uniform sphere of the stated radius whose gravity follows the inverse-square law with the stated surface value; the orbits are circular and the atmosphere, the Moon and the Sun are ignored. All of the change of the total (kinetic plus potential) energy of the satellite is supplied by the engines; the loss of mass of the burnt propellant is neglected.
Step 4. The added sentence ("On an earlier flight, the satellite also carried a further 95 kg of instruments.") gives 95 kg. This quantity has no path to the target: the satellite carried the further instruments on an earlier flight, for that flight only; on the stated flight it has only its stated mass. It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.
Step 5. Approach: The work of the engines equals the change of the total mechanical energy of the satellite. For a circular orbit the total energy is minus the kinetic energy. Find the two orbit radii and the difference of the two total energies.
Step 6. Radius of a circular orbit, r = R_E + altitude. The altitude is measured from the surface, while the law of gravity needs the distance from the centre of the Earth. r1 = Re + h1  (SI units). r1 = (6.371e+06) + (4e+05) = 6.771e+06 (SI) = 6.771e+06 m.
Step 7. Radius of a circular orbit, r = R_E + altitude. The final orbit is treated in the same way as the initial orbit. r2 = Re + h2  (SI units). r2 = (6.371e+06) + (1.2e+06) = 7.571e+06 (SI) = 7.571e+06 m.
Step 8. Work-energy theorem with the total energy of a circular orbit, E = -G M m/(2 r) = -m g0 R^2/(2 r). The engines supply the change of the total energy; for a circular orbit the centripetal condition makes the kinetic energy half of the magnitude of the potential energy, so E is minus the kinetic energy. W = m*g0*Re**2*(1/r1 - 1/r2)/2  (SI units). W = (850)*(9.8)*(6.371e+06)**2*(1/(6.771e+06) - 1/(7.571e+06))/2 = 2.638e+09 (SI) = 2.638e+06 kJ.
Step 9. Check: The work is positive and is less than the change of the potential energy alone, because the kinetic energy decreases as the satellite goes up; it vanishes when the two altitudes are equal.
Step 10. Answer: work done by the engines: 2.638e+06 kJ.

Step 2. Given: rho1 = 1.2 kg/m³ (density of the air; given); c1 = 343 m/s (speed of sound in the air; given); rho2 = 998 kg/m³ (density of the water; given); c2 = 1482 m/s (speed of sound in the water; given); Ii = 0.012 W/m² (intensity of the incident sound wave; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The waves are plane and harmonic, the surface is flat and horizontal, the incidence is normal, and both fluids are uniform and lossless. The pressure and the normal velocity of the fluid are continuous across the surface, and the water is deep, so that nothing returns from below.
Step 4. The added sentence ("Before the pressure is measured, the intensity of the sound from the second loudspeaker is increased by 0.003 W/m².") gives 0.003 W/m². This quantity has no path to the target: turning up the second loudspeaker changes the sound at the boathouse wall; the incident wave from the first loudspeaker keeps its stated intensity and the two fluids are as stated. It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.
Step 5. Approach: At a boundary between two fluids the pressure and the normal velocity are continuous, so the transmitted power fraction depends only on the ratio of the acoustic impedances. Find the ratio, the power fraction, the transmitted intensity and then the pressure amplitude in the water.
Step 6. Specific acoustic impedance of a fluid, Z = rho c, and the ratio Z2/Z1. The reflection at the surface is decided by how well the impedances of the two fluids match. rz = (rho2*c2)/(rho1*c1)  (SI units). rz = ((998)*(1482))/((1.2)*(343)) = 3593 (SI) = 3593.
Step 7. Intensity transmission coefficient at normal incidence, T = 4 Z1 Z2/(Z1 + Z2)^2 = 4 r/(1 + r)^2. Continuity of pressure and velocity gives the fraction of the incident power that enters the water. tr = 4*rz/(1 + rz)**2  (SI units). tr = 4*(3593)/(1 + (3593))**2 = 0.001113 (SI) = 0.001113.
Step 8. Transmitted intensity is the transmission coefficient times the incident intensity. The intensity of the incident wave is given, and a fraction T of it is transmitted. It = tr*Ii  (SI units). It = (0.001113)*(0.012) = 1.335e-05 (SI) = 1.335e-05 W/m².
Step 9. Intensity of a plane wave, I = p^2/(2 Z), so p = sqrt(2 Z I). The question asks for a pressure amplitude in the water, so the impedance of the water converts the transmitted intensity. pt = sqrt(2*rho2*c2*It)  (SI units). pt = sqrt(2*(998)*(1482)*(1.335e-05)) = 6.284 (SI) = 6.284 Pa.
Step 10. Check: The transmission coefficient is tiny, about a tenth of a percent, yet the pressure amplitude in the water is nearly twice the incident one; the intensity transmitted never exceeds the incident intensity.
Step 11. Answer: pressure amplitude of the sound wave in the water: 6.284 Pa.

Step 6. Definition of intensity for a point source, I = P/(4 pi r^2). Without absorption the intensity is the power divided by the area of the sphere. I0 = P/area  (SI units). I0 = (40)/(4.524e+04) = 0.0008842 (SI) = 0.0008842 W/m².
Step 7. Exponential absorption of the intensity along the path, I = I0 exp(-alpha r). The air removes a constant fraction of the intensity per unit path, so the spreading result is multiplied by this factor. I = I0*exp(-alpha*r)  (SI units). I = (0.0008842)*exp(-(0.004)*(60)) = 0.0006955 (SI) = 0.0006955 W/m².
Step 8. Check: The result is smaller than the value without absorption and tends to it as alpha tends to zero; it falls faster than 1/r^2 at large distance.
Step 9. Answer: sound intensity at the observer: 0.0006955 W/m².

steps.why: The thermal strain is driven by the rise of the temperature of the strip.

steps.why: Only the mismatch of the free thermal strains of the two layers bends the strip.

steps.why: The stiffness of the section and the position of its neutral axis depend on the ratio of the moduli.

steps.principle: Timoshenko bimetal formula for equal layers, curvature = 24 da dT/(h Dn)
steps.why: The curvature is the thermal mismatch strain divided by the thickness, reduced by the stiffness factor.

items: The strip is a thin beam of two bonded layers of equal thickness and the same width, with linear elastic behaviour and constants independent of temperature, and its curvature is small.
One end of the strip is clamped with the strip horizontal and unstressed at the initial temperature; the whole strip is heated uniformly and slowly, and no load acts on it.

steps.text: The layer with the larger expansion coefficient wants to be longer than the other, so the bonded strip bends. For two layers of equal thickness the curvature follows from the balance of force and moment in the section; the free end then moves through the curvature times the length squared over two.

The added sentence ("The strip has a width of 6 mm.") gives the width of the strip, q = 6 mm (= 0.006 in SI). It belongs to the system, so it may enter intermediate relations; only the final answer must not depend on it.
Relation 1 that contains q: bending moment of the layers M = q * (moment per unit width).
Relation 2 that contains q: bending stiffness of the section = q * (stiffness per unit width).
Relation 3 that contains q: curvature = M / stiffness.
q cancels: the expression simplifies to -12*E1*E2*L**2*(T - T0)*(a1 - a2)/(h*(12*E1*E2 + (E1 + E2)**2)), and its derivative with respect to q is 0. The answer is the same for every q: 12.22 mm.
For equal moduli the stiffness factor is 16 and the curvature is 3 da dT/(2 h), the classical result; the deflection grows with the square of the length and falls as the strip gets thicker.
vertical deflection of the free end: 12.22 mm

Step 1. Find the activity of the daughter isotope, in Bq.
Step 2. Given: A0 = 4000 Bq (activity of the parent isotope at the start; given); Tp = 66 h (half-life of the parent isotope; given); Td = 6 h (half-life of the daughter isotope; given); t = 24 h (time since the start; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The parent decays only to the daughter, and the daughter decays to a stable nuclide; no daughter is present at the start, and nothing is removed from the column or added to it afterwards. Each decay follows the exponential law with the constant decay constant ln 2 divided by the half-life.
Step 4. Approach: The parent decays exponentially and feeds the daughter, which decays itself. Find the two decay constants, the factor that couples them, and then the daughter activity from the difference of the two exponentials.
Step 5. Decay constant from the half-life, lambda = ln 2/T. The daughter is treated in the same way as the parent. ld = log(2)/Td  (SI units). ld = log(2)/(2.16e+04) = 3.209e-05 (SI) = 3.209e-05 1/s.
Step 6. Decay constant from the half-life, lambda = ln 2/T. The decay of each isotope is exponential, and the half-life fixes the constant. lp = log(2)/Tp  (SI units). lp = log(2)/(2.376e+05) = 2.917e-06 (SI) = 2.917e-06 1/s.
Step 7. Coupling factor of a two-member chain, lambda_d/(lambda_d - lambda_p). The rate of production of the daughter is the activity of the parent, and solving the coupled equations gives this factor. rr = ld/(ld - lp)  (SI units). rr = (3.209e-05)/((3.209e-05) - (2.917e-06)) = 1.1 (SI) = 1.1.
Step 8. Bateman solution for the daughter with no daughter at the start, A_d = A_0 lambda_d/(lambda_d - lambda_p) (exp(-lambda_p t) - exp(-lambda_d t)). The daughter is produced by the parent and removed by its own decay, so its activity is the difference of the two exponentials. Ad = A0*rr*(exp(-lp*t) - exp(-ld*t))  (SI units). Ad = (4000)*(1.1)*(exp(-(2.917e-06)*(8.64e+04)) - exp(-(3.209e-05)*(8.64e+04))) = 3145 (SI) = 3145 Bq.
Step 9. Check: The daughter activity is zero at the start, rises to a maximum, and then follows the parent; it never exceeds the parent activity at the time of the maximum when the parent is longer lived.
Step 10. Answer: activity of the daughter isotope: 3145 Bq.

items: The gas is ideal and in thermal equilibrium, the molecules are hard spheres of the stated effective diameter with Maxwell-distributed speeds, and all of the molecules move.

steps.text: A molecule collides about once per mean free path travelled, so the collision rate is the mean speed over the mean free path. Find the cross-section, the mean free path, the mean speed, and then the ratio.

steps.description: collision cross-section of a molecule
steps.principle: Collision cross-section of hard spheres of diameter d, sigma = pi d^2
steps.why: Two molecules collide when their centres come within one diameter, so the target area is this circle.

steps.description: mean speed of the molecules
steps.principle: Mean speed of a Maxwell gas, v = sqrt(8 k T/(pi m))
steps.why: The distance travelled each second is the mean speed.

steps.description: mean free path
steps.principle: Mean free path, lambda = k T/(sqrt(2) sigma p), from n = p/(k T) and lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) n sigma)
steps.why: The factor sqrt(2) accounts for the motion of the other molecules; the ideal-gas law gives the number density.

steps.description: collision rate of one molecule
steps.principle: Collision rate as the mean speed divided by the mean free path, z = v/lambda
steps.why: The molecule travels one mean free path between two successive collisions.

steps.text: The rate grows linearly with the pressure and as the square root of the temperature; for nitrogen at atmospheric pressure it is of the order of several billion per second.

Step 2. Given: p = 80 kPa (pressure of the gas; given); T = 300 K (temperature of the gas; given); d = 370 pm (effective diameter of a molecule; given); m = 28 u (mass of a molecule; given); kB = 1.381e-23 J/K (Boltzmann constant, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The gas is ideal and in thermal equilibrium, the molecules are hard spheres of the stated effective diameter with Maxwell-distributed speeds, and all of the molecules move. Only collisions between molecules are counted; the mean free path is much shorter than the vessel, so that collisions with the walls are negligible.
Step 4. Approach: A molecule collides about once per mean free path travelled, so the collision rate is the mean speed over the mean free path. Find the cross-section, the mean free path, the mean speed, and then the ratio.
Step 5. Collision cross-section of hard spheres of diameter d, sigma = pi d^2. Two molecules collide when their centres come within one diameter, so the target area is this circle. sig = pi*d**2  (SI units). sig = pi*(3.7e-10)**2 = 4.301e-19 (SI) = 4.301e-19 m².
Step 6. Mean speed of a Maxwell gas, v = sqrt(8 k T/(pi m)). The distance travelled each second is the mean speed. vbar = sqrt(8*kB*T/(pi*m))  (SI units). vbar = sqrt(8*(1.381e-23)*(300)/(pi*(4.65e-26))) = 476.3 (SI) = 476.3 m/s.
Step 7. Mean free path, lambda = k T/(sqrt(2) sigma p), from n = p/(k T) and lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) n sigma). The factor sqrt(2) accounts for the motion of the other molecules; the ideal-gas law gives the number density. lam = kB*T/(sqrt(2)*sig*p)  (SI units). lam = (1.381e-23)*(300)/(sqrt(2)*(4.301e-19)*(8e+04)) = 8.514e-08 (SI) = 8.514e-08 m.
Step 8. Collision rate as the mean speed divided by the mean free path, z = v/lambda. The molecule travels one mean free path between two successive collisions. z = vbar/lam  (SI units). z = (476.3)/(8.514e-08) = 5.595e+09 (SI) = 5.595 GHz.
Step 9. Check: The rate grows linearly with the pressure and as the square root of the temperature; for nitrogen at atmospheric pressure it is of the order of several billion per second.
Step 10. Answer: collisions per second of one molecule: 5.595 GHz.

steps.principle: Collision cross-section of hard spheres of diameter d, sigma = pi d^2
steps.why: Two molecules collide when their centres come within one diameter, so the target area is this circle.

steps.description: mean speed of the molecules
steps.principle: Mean speed of a Maxwell gas, v = sqrt(8 k T/(pi m))
steps.why: The distance travelled each second is the mean speed.

steps.description: mean free path
steps.principle: Mean free path, lambda = k T/(sqrt(2) sigma p), from n = p/(k T) and lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) n sigma)
steps.why: The factor sqrt(2) accounts for the motion of the other molecules; the ideal-gas law gives the number density.

steps.description: collision rate of one molecule
steps.principle: Collision rate as the mean speed divided by the mean free path, z = v/lambda
steps.why: The molecule travels one mean free path between two successive collisions.

steps.text: The rate grows linearly with the pressure and as the square root of the temperature; for nitrogen at atmospheric pressure it is of the order of several billion per second.

Step 3. Step 5. Natural logarithm of the ratio of the initial to the final depth. The depth follows h = h0 exp(-t/tau), so the time for a given fall depends on the logarithm of the depth ratio. lr = log(h0/h1)  (SI units). lr = log((0.4)/(0.25)) = 0.47 (SI) = 0.47.

Step 9. Answer: time for the oil to fall to the final depth: 16.75 min.

steps.text: The load voltage is the rectified secondary voltage minus the two forward drops, but only while the diodes conduct. Find the peak voltage of the secondary, the phase at which conduction starts, then average the load voltage over a cycle.

steps.description: peak voltage of the secondary
steps.principle: Peak of a sinusoid from its rms value, Vp = sqrt(2) Vrms, and the turns ratio of an ideal transformer, Vs = Vm / n
steps.why: The ideal transformer divides the mains rms voltage by the turns ratio; the peak voltage of the secondary is root two times its rms value.

steps.description: phase at which the diodes start to conduct
steps.principle: Conduction condition of a diode pair, Vp sin(th) = 2 Vd
steps.why: Two diodes conduct at a time, so the rectified voltage must exceed two forward drops before any current flows; this gives the phase th0 at which conduction starts.

steps.description: average voltage across the load
steps.principle: Average of the load voltage, (1 / pi) integral from th0 to pi - th0 of (Vp sin th - 2 Vd) d(th)
steps.why: The rectified waveform repeats every half cycle and is zero outside the conduction interval, so the average over a half cycle is the integral over the interval divided by pi; it evaluates to (2 / pi) (Vp cos th0 - 2 Vd (pi/2 - th0)).

steps.text: Limiting case: with zero forward drop the average is the textbook 2 Vp / pi. The average is less than that by about the two drops times the conducting fraction of the cycle. Order of magnitude: an 80 V peak gives about 50 V.
average voltage across the load: 50.38 V

The rectified waveform repeats every half cycle and is zero outside the conduction interval, so the average over a half cycle is the integral over the interval divided by pi; it evaluates to (2 / pi) (Vp cos th0 - 2 Vd (pi/2 - th0)). Vavg = (2/pi)*(Vp*cos(th0) - 2*Vd*(pi/2 - th0))  (SI units). Vavg = (2/pi)*((81.32)*cos((0.01722)) - 2*(0.7)*(pi/2 - (0.01722))) = 50.38 (SI) = 50.38 V.

steps.description: peak voltage of the secondary

steps.description: phase at which the diodes start to conduct

steps.description: average voltage across the load

steps.description: average voltage across the load

items.description: number of turns of the primary winding
items.name: Np

items.description: number of turns of the secondary winding
items.name: Ns

items: The flux links every turn of both windings and the magnetising current, the leakage inductance and the core loss are negligible, so the currents are in the inverse ratio of the turns and the load is a resistor that takes the stated power at the stated voltage.
The only losses are the heat in the two windings, each of the stated resistance, and the currents are steady sinusoidal rms values.

steps.text: The windings dissipate heat in proportion to the squares of their currents. Find the secondary current from the delivered power and voltage, the primary current from the turns ratio, then add the two winding heats.

steps.description: rms current in the secondary winding
steps.principle: Electrical power of a resistive load, P = Vs Is
steps.why: The load takes the stated power at the stated rms voltage, so the current in the secondary winding, which is the load current, is the power divided by the voltage.

steps.description: rms current in the primary winding
steps.principle: Ampere-turn balance of an ideal transformer, Np Ip = Ns Is
steps.why: With negligible magnetising current the two windings produce equal and opposite magnetomotive forces, so the currents are in the inverse ratio of the turns.

steps.description: power dissipated in the two windings
steps.principle: Joule heating in each winding, P = I^2 R, summed over the two windings
steps.why: The heat in a winding is the square of its current times its resistance, and the only losses are in the two windings.

steps.text: Power balance: the input power is the sum of the delivered power and the two winding losses. The primary loss is smaller than the secondary loss would be if the secondary current flowed in the primary resistance, by the square of the turns ratio.
power dissipated as heat in the two windings: 32 W

Step 1. Find the power dissipated as heat in the two windings, in W.
Step 2. Given: P = 480 W (power delivered to the load; given); Vs = 24 V (rms voltage across the load; given); Np = 1200 (number of turns of the primary winding; given); Ns = 120 (number of turns of the secondary winding; given); Rp = 3 Ω (resistance of the primary winding; given); Rs = 0.05 Ω (resistance of the secondary winding; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The flux links every turn of both windings and the magnetising current, the leakage inductance and the core loss are negligible, so the currents are in the inverse ratio of the turns and the load is a resistor that takes the stated power at the stated voltage. The only losses are the heat in the two windings, each of the stated resistance, and the currents are steady sinusoidal rms values.
Step 4. Approach: The windings dissipate heat in proportion to the squares of their currents. Find the secondary current from the delivered power and voltage, the primary current from the turns ratio, then add the two winding heats.
Step 5. Electrical power of a resistive load, P = Vs Is. The load takes the stated power at the stated rms voltage, so the current in the secondary winding, which is the load current, is the power divided by the voltage. Is = P/Vs  (SI units). Is = (480)/(24) = 20 (SI) = 20 A.
Step 6. Ampere-turn balance of an ideal transformer, Np Ip = Ns Is. With negligible magnetising current the two windings produce equal and opposite magnetomotive forces, so the currents are in the inverse ratio of the turns. Ip = Is*Ns/Np  (SI units). Ip = (20)*(120)/(1200) = 2 (SI) = 2 A.
Step 7. Joule heating in each winding, P = I^2 R, summed over the two windings. The heat in a winding is the square of its current times its resistance, and the only losses are in the two windings. Ploss = Is**2*Rs + Ip**2*Rp  (SI units). Ploss = (20)**2*(0.05) + (2)**2*(3) = 32 (SI) = 32 W.
Step 8. Check: Power balance: the input power is the sum of the delivered power and the two winding losses. The primary loss is smaller than the secondary loss would be if the secondary current flowed in the primary resistance, by the square of the turns ratio.
Step 9. Answer: power dissipated as heat in the two windings: 32 W.

The capacitor sees the two resistors as a battery of fixed voltage with the parallel combination of the resistors in series, so it charges exponentially towards the open-circuit voltage of the divider. Find the Thevenin resistance, the time constant, then the time to the stated fraction.

steps.description: Thevenin resistance seen by the capacitor
steps.principle: Thevenin resistance of the divider, Rth = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2)
steps.why: With the battery replaced by its negligible internal resistance, the capacitor sees the two resistors in parallel.

steps.description: time constant of the charging
steps.principle: Time constant of an RC circuit, tau = Rth C
steps.why: The capacitor charges through the Thevenin resistance, so the time constant is that resistance times the capacitance.

steps.description: time for the capacitor voltage to reach the stated fraction of its final value
steps.principle: Exponential approach to the final value, v = vf (1 - exp(-t / tau)), so t = -tau ln(1 - p)
steps.why: The capacitor voltage rises as a fraction p = 1 - exp(-t / tau) of the final value vf, the open-circuit voltage of the divider; since the fraction is taken of that final value, the battery emf cancels.

steps.text: Limiting case: for a fraction of 1 - 1/e the time is one time constant. The result does not depend on the battery emf, and is shorter than R1 C ln(1/(1 - p)) because the parallel combination is smaller than R1.

items.description: number of turns of the solenoid
items.name: N

items.description: permeability of free space, a stated constant

items: The permeability of free space has the stated value and the solenoid has no core.
The solenoid is long compared with its radius, so its field is uniform inside and negligible outside, and its winding has negligible resistance.

The battery is ideal and the current has reached its steady value before the switch opens; when it opens, the whole current of the solenoid passes through the discharge resistor and no energy is radiated.

steps.text: While the switch is closed the solenoid carries a steady current set by the battery and the series resistor; when the switch opens that current keeps flowing through the second resistor and its magnetic energy is turned into heat. Find the inductance, the current, then the stored energy.

steps.description: steady current in the solenoid
steps.principle: Ohm's law in the steady state, I0 = V / R1
steps.why: In the steady state an ideal solenoid has no voltage across it, so the whole battery voltage drops over the series resistor and the second resistor carries no current.

steps.description: inductance of the solenoid
steps.principle: Inductance of a long air-cored solenoid, L = mu0 N^2 pi a^2 / ell
steps.why: The solenoid is long, so its field is uniform inside; the flux linkage per unit current gives the inductance.

steps.description: energy released as heat in the discharge resistor
steps.principle: Energy stored in an inductor, E = L I0^2 / 2
steps.why: After the switch opens the current decays through the second resistor, which dissipates all the stored magnetic energy (the integral of I^2 R from the exponential decay gives L I0^2 / 2 whatever the resistance), so the heat equals the energy stored at the moment of opening.

steps.text: Dimensional check: henry times ampere squared is a joule. The heat does not depend on the value of the second resistor, which only sets how fast the current decays. Order of magnitude: millijoules for a few-millihenry coil at a few amperes.

steps.description: steady current in the solenoid

steps.description: inductance of the solenoid

steps.description: energy released as heat in the discharge resistor

Approach: While the switch is closed the solenoid carries a steady current set by the battery and the series resistor; when the switch opens that current keeps flowing through the second resistor and its magnetic energy is turned into heat. items: The speed of sound has the stated constant value in the still air and does not depend on the frequency.

The lorry and the trolley move at constant speeds along one straight line through the post, the air is still, and the flat rear panel of the lorry sends every wave crest straight back with no change of frequency in its own rest frame.

steps.text: Sound moves through the still air, so each Doppler shift depends on the speeds of the moving parties relative to the air. The receding lorry first acts as an observer that moves away from the oncoming sound, then as a source that moves away from the recorder, and the retreating recorder finally moves along with the reflected sound. Find the frequency at the lorry, the frequency of the reflected sound, then the difference from the note.

steps.description: frequency of the sound that reaches the lorry
steps.principle: Doppler effect for a moving observer and a source at rest, f1 = f (c - w) / c
steps.why: The lorry moves away from the post at w, in the direction of travel of the sound, so it meets the wave crests less often than a lorry at rest would.

steps.description: frequency of the reflected sound that the recorder picks up
steps.principle: Doppler effect for a receding source and an observer moving with the wave, f2 = f1 (c - v) / (c + w)
steps.why: The lorry sends back the frequency f1 while it moves away from the recorder at w, which lengthens the wavelength to (c + w) / f1, and the trolley retreats at v in the direction of travel of the reflected sound, so the observer term is c - v.

steps.description: amount by which the frequency of the reflected sound lies below the frequency of the note
steps.principle: Frequency difference, df = f - f2
steps.why: The question asks how far the frequency of the reflected sound lies below the note; it is lower because the lorry and the trolley both move away from the sources of the sound they receive.

steps.text: Limiting cases: with the lorry and the trolley at rest the reflected sound has the frequency of the note and the difference is zero. For speeds that are small compared with the speed of sound the difference is about f (2 w + v) / c, so it grows with either speed and the lorry counts twice as much as the trolley.

The lorry and the trolley move at constant speeds along one straight line through the post, the air is still, and the flat rear panel of the lorry sends every wave crest straight back with no change of frequency in its own rest frame.

steps.text: The added sentence ("Before the trolley sets off, a conveyor belt is started that carries the toolbox along the trolley directly away from the lorry at 5.3 m/s.") gives 5.3 m/s. This quantity has no path to the target: a belt that carries the toolbox along the trolley moves the toolbox only; the recorder keeps the stated speed of the trolley, so the reflected sound and its shift are the stated ones. It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.

Sound moves through the still air, so each Doppler shift depends on the speeds of the moving parties relative to the air. The receding lorry first acts as an observer that moves away from the oncoming sound, then as a source that moves away from the recorder, and the retreating recorder finally moves along with the reflected sound. Find the frequency at the lorry, the frequency of the reflected sound, then the difference from the note.

steps.description: frequency of the sound that reaches the lorry
steps.principle: Doppler effect for a moving observer and a source at rest, f1 = f (c - w) / c
steps.why: The lorry moves away from the post at w, in the direction of travel of the sound, so it meets the wave crests less often than a lorry at rest would.

steps.description: frequency of the reflected sound that the recorder picks up
steps.principle: Doppler effect for a receding source and an observer moving with the wave, f2 = f1 (c - v) / (c + w)
steps.why: The lorry sends back the frequency f1 while it moves away from the recorder at w, which lengthens the wavelength to (c + w) / f1, and the trolley retreats at v in the direction of travel of the reflected sound, so the observer term is c - v.

steps.description: amount by which the frequency of the reflected sound lies below the frequency of the note
steps.principle: Frequency difference, df = f - f2
steps.why: The question asks how far the frequency of the reflected sound lies below the note; it is lower because the lorry and the trolley both move away from the sources of the sound they receive.

steps.text: Limiting cases: with the lorry and the trolley at rest the reflected sound has the frequency of the note and the difference is zero. For speeds that are small compared with the speed of sound the difference is about f (2 w + v) / c, so it grows with either speed and the lorry counts twice as much as the trolley.

The rod is thin, so longitudinal waves travel along it at sqrt(Y / rho); it is clamped exactly at its middle and vibrates in its fundamental longitudinal mode with free ends, and the air in the tube is driven at that frequency by a disc on one end.
The dust collects at the displacement nodes of the standing wave in the tube, which are half a wavelength apart.

steps.text: The rod vibrates like a bar with both ends free and a node at its middle, so a half wavelength of the longitudinal wave in the rod fits its length; the rod then drives the air at that frequency and the dust marks half-wavelength intervals of the sound in air. steps.description: speed of longitudinal waves along the rod
steps.principle: Speed of longitudinal waves in a thin rod, v = sqrt(Y / rho)
steps.why: The rod is thin, so a longitudinal pulse travels at the square root of Young's modulus over the density.

steps.description: frequency of the fundamental longitudinal vibration of the rod
steps.principle: Fundamental longitudinal mode of a free-free rod clamped at its middle, f = v / (2 L)
steps.why: The middle is a displacement node and the two free ends are antinodes, so the rod length is half a wavelength of the longitudinal wave.

steps.description: wavelength of the sound in the air of the tube
steps.principle: Wavelength of a wave, lambda = c / f
steps.why: The disc forces the air in the tube at the frequency of the rod, so the sound in the air has the speed of sound divided by that frequency.

steps.description: spacing of adjacent dust heaps
steps.principle: Adjacent nodes of a standing wave are half a wavelength apart, d = lambda / 2
steps.why: The dust is shaken away from the displacement antinodes and collects at the nodes, which are half a wavelength apart.

steps.text: Order of magnitude: aluminium carries sound at about five kilometres per second, so a rod of about a metre rings at a few kilohertz and the heaps are a few centimetres apart. The spacing is proportional to the rod length and independent of its cross-section.

The rod is thin, so longitudinal waves travel along it at sqrt(Y / rho); it is clamped exactly at its middle and vibrates in its fundamental longitudinal mode with free ends, and the air in the tube is driven at that frequency by a disc on one end.
The dust collects at the displacement nodes of the standing wave in the tube, which are half a wavelength apart.

The rod vibrates like a bar with both ends free and a node at its middle, so a half wavelength of the longitudinal wave in the rod fits its length; the rod then drives the air at that frequency and the dust marks half-wavelength intervals of the sound in air. Find the wave speed in the rod, its vibration frequency, the wavelength in air, then the spacing.

steps.description: speed of longitudinal waves along the rod
steps.principle: Speed of longitudinal waves in a thin rod, v = sqrt(Y / rho)
steps.why: The rod is thin, so a longitudinal pulse travels at the square root of Young's modulus over the density.

steps.description: frequency of the fundamental longitudinal vibration of the rod
steps.principle: Fundamental longitudinal mode of a free-free rod clamped at its middle, f = v / (2 L)
steps.why: The middle is a displacement node and the two free ends are antinodes, so the rod length is half a wavelength of the longitudinal wave.

steps.description: wavelength of the sound in the air of the tube
steps.principle: Wavelength of a wave, lambda = c / f
steps.why: The disc forces the air in the tube at the frequency of the rod, so the sound in the air has the speed of sound divided by that frequency.

steps.description: spacing of adjacent dust heaps
steps.principle: Adjacent nodes of a standing wave are half a wavelength apart, d = lambda / 2
steps.why: The dust is shaken away from the displacement antinodes and collects at the nodes, which are half a wavelength apart.

steps.text: Order of magnitude: aluminium carries sound at about five kilometres per second, so a rod of about a metre rings at a few kilohertz and the heaps are a few centimetres apart. The spacing is proportional to the rod length and independent of its cross-section.

Step 3. Assumptions: The speed of sound in the air of the tube has the stated constant value.
